Heaven Devouring adds one percentage point per target each second: 1%, 2%, 3%, up to 100%. A warp deals HP damage based on 10% of the caster's maximum Qi, resets that target to zero, then starts again at 1% next second. Leaving or ending the domain clears accumulated chance.
screen.immortal_cultivation_mod.npc.dial: Seeking a spell, traveler? Inspect these jade slips before choosing your path.
Twelve different spells in my pack. Take your time choosing.
Each scroll has a marked price. Pay the spirit stones and it is yours.
Buying a scroll is only the beginning. Understanding it takes your own effort.
If a scroll sells out today, return after the next dawn for fresh stock.
Choose a spell that suits your foundations; power alone is not enough.
The scrolls I carry must suit my cultivation realm.
A Qi Refining trader carries useful minor spells, not empty promises of heavenly power.
Foundation Establishment opens longer roads and access to more advanced spells.
Obtaining and safeguarding Golden Core spells takes considerable work.
Stronger merchants find advanced scrolls more often, while still keeping practical minor spells.
Sect paths and market roads always bring requests to carry jade slips.
Every spell has its own lineage. Finding one that suits you is a fortunate meeting.
Strengthen your foundations before forcing yourself to study an unsuitable spell.
A trader lives by trust. A sold scroll will not magically reappear in my pack today.
Return tomorrow if you can. Fresh stock may contain the spell you seek.
guidance.immortal_cultivation_mod.chapte: Wandering Spell Merchants

Spell Merchants wander the Overworld in violet robes. Each carries twelve distinct spell scrolls, limited by the merchant's realm; stronger merchants favor advanced spells. Open Trade through their interaction menu and pay the listed spirit-stone price. Sold scrolls stay sold until the next in-game day. Buying a scroll does not learn it: use its normal learning process and meet its requirements.
message.immortal_cultivation_mod.debug.n: Your previous life has ended. A new life begins.
screen.immortal_cultivation_mod.debug_ag: Reducing remaining lifespan to 0 starts a new life and resets cultivation.
guidance.immortal_cultivation_mod.chapte: A New Life at Zero

Use /cultivationdebug set <player> age 0 to end that player's current life and reset cultivation, methods and spells through the existing new-life rules. The cultivation debug editor also starts a new life when its age-minus control reaches zero or below. Positive values only adjust remaining lifespan.
Heavenly Thunder Resonance

Violet flames carry turquoise branches beneath slowly turning thundercloud currents. Enemies within six blocks of one another exchange automatic arcs each second. After three seconds of exposure, charged enemies periodically release extra branches; isolated enemies can draw a cloud discharge. No attack is required. Each caster can deal domain lightning damage to a victim at most once per second.
Ten Thousand Mountains' Weight

Profound Mountain Edge-Shattering forms heavy earth-gold strata and floating stone. Enemies throughout the domain are slowed and gently pressed downward. Movement stirs dust and golden cracks; mountain shadows gather above them. Close groups intensify the pressure visuals without destroying terrain.
Eternal Abyssal Current

Cold-Tide fills its domain with deep-blue spiritual water. Each block actually travelled inside adds one Damp stack, capped at eight. Back-and-forth travel counts; standing still and teleports do not. Damp lasts ten seconds and continued movement refreshes it. Higher stacks show denser water currents. Steps leave world-anchored ripples that expand and fade. Existing Damp interactions with water and ice spells remain. The caster still heals 0.2% of maximum HP each second, capped at four, and extinguishes fire.
Ice Remembers

Cold Cry Ice-Seizing grows ice more slowly over targets with higher maximum HP; wounds do not change the rate. Full buildup takes twice the square root of maximum HP in seconds, at least five seconds: 100 max HP takes 20 seconds. Outside the domain, partial ice melts over at least a minute per full coat and four times more slowly than buildup. Re-entry resumes from the remainder. Reloading preserves it.
Five Minutes in Ice

Targets fully frozen by Cold Cry Ice-Seizing cannot move, attack, cast spells or use beast abilities. The domain maintains the lock; after its last contact, full freezing lasts five minutes even if the caster stops. Then the ice shatters and actions resume. Slimes and magma cubes are immune to this domain's frost, slow and full freeze.
Ashes into Life

Orange-red spiritual fire rises beneath enemies and breaks into gold embers that return to the caster's chest. Flame contact burns each second and restores health equal to 5% of actual HP damage dealt. Blocked damage yields no free vitality. These flames do not ignite terrain.
Silent Winter

Pale blue crystalline flames spread frost from feet through legs, torso, arms and head, following each mob's actual animated model. Thin transparent frost grows at the same maximum-HP base rate as red lilies: max(5, twice the square root of target maximum HP) seconds to full coverage. A 100-max-HP target takes 20 seconds; 400 takes 40 seconds. Wounds do not change this rate. Slowness builds from I to IV as coverage increases. Full coverage locks movement, attacks, spells and beast abilities for five minutes after the last domain contact. Partial ice slowly thaws outside and resumes from the remainder on reentry. Slimes and magma cubes are immune. Each second the caster heals 0.2% of maximum HP, capped at four, and extinguishes fire. When freezing ends, the coating cracks and shatters into fragments sampled from the real model surface. It is never a separate ice cube.
Bone Bell

Bone Bell compares innate attack plus trained physical attack plus one point for every twenty maximum HP. Bone-tempering health gains count; wounds and weapon attack modifiers do not. Strictly weaker bodies suffer thirty percent movement suppression, separate from ordinary Slowness and its cleanses. Equal or stronger bodies are unaffected. Ivory waves, foot dust and deep bell vibrations express physical presence without gravity. Your own rings are hidden in first-person and remain visible in third-person.
Nether Procession

Nine Nether Corpse-Refining wears violet-black flame and ghost-green wisps; hits leave smoky decaying marks. Nether Procession has no additional passive domain damage, Wither, Weakness, suppression or healing.
Solar Furnace

Solar motes erupt into golden-white pillars each second. Base damage is caster maximum HP × current Sun Energy percentage value ÷ 1000: 10%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% Sun Energy deal 1%, 2.5%, 5%, 7.5% and 10% of the caster's maximum HP per pillar. Current HP and target HP do not set this damage. Zero Sun Energy deals no pillar damage. Suppression and existing defenses apply. Brightness, density and heat shimmer rise with current Sun Energy.
Blood Returning to Its Source

Flowers follow feet, limbs, torso and head, not a bounding box. At full coverage, each second drains ordinary domain HP damage and twice that amount of real Qi. Actual HP lost and Qi removed return to the caster, capped by its maxima. Partial coverage, leaving range or stopping the domain prevents drain. Hit counts are saved separately per caster and target, resetting when flowers fully wilt. Misses, fully blocked hits and passive lily drain add no stacks. Overlapping domains use the strongest growth multiplier, without stacking base growth or drain pulses.
Shadows Between Lives

On a Reincarnation proc, an open black-and-white wheel with paired inner curves briefly appears beneath opposing body currents. Two translucent copies of the enemy's actual model separate to either side and trail its movement. Orbiting particles collapse when ten seconds end. Another proc adds a level and refreshes ten seconds; an older, longer lower-level effect can resume afterward.
Read the Colors of Protection

Shield colors follow their source: Body-Protecting Qi pearl white; Dielang blue; Solid Stone brown; Blood Qi Pill pink; Mystic Stone amber; Flowing Wind mint; Bloodfiend crimson; Spirit Mirror lavender; Primordial Barrier cyan; Black Tortoise Mirror teal; bone ivory. Thin Gold talismans are yellow, Golden Body orange, and old untyped talismans muted violet. Stacked shields retain separate colored sections with one total. Damage drains its own section; broken or expired sections disappear.
Wind Along the Rift

Void Breaking retains its original mint-white palette. Idle currents, floating wind fragments and red ground haze are absent. Wind paths change every 1.6 seconds; confirmed hits alone show brief crossing cuts, scene refraction, dust and upward pressure. Domain cutting damage is halved for both players and NPCs. No terrain edits are created. Devouring instead folds the victim's silhouette inward, contracts to a black point and bursts into dark fragments.
Wood in Bloom and Decay

Evergreen's green-gold pollen drifts irregularly. Contact raises real collidable oak-log spikes with leaves, bark and green veins. Over two seconds the wood cracks and withers, dissolving in stages during the final half-second. Further contacts may erupt again. Existing terrain and later player edits are preserved.
screen.immortal_cultivation_mod.settings: Show the mod's Overworld night sky. Turn off to use the shader pack's sky. Changes apply immediately.
spell.immortal_cultivation_mod.yanmie_we: One Whom Annihilation Has Not Finished

Passive curse. At 5% HP, restores full health once per life. Restored HP is black; healing is blocked until death. Rescue has a 30-minute online cooldown that survives death. Black runes spread outward from the chest without harming their host. After blooming, accepted attacks infect enemies and accelerate growth. Infected targets lose Qi each second. Base HP corrosion is 1% of their maximum HP per second at full rune coverage, scaled down for partial coverage; defenses still apply. They cannot heal. Contact only spreads up to half the source coverage. Meditation removes 1 percentage point per minute and grants no cultivation or method experience until fully cleansed. Activate to inspect the curse.
curse.annihilation.acquired: Innate ability awakened: One Whom Annihilation Has Not Finished. Something within the bottle has chosen your body.
curse.annihilation.rescued: The parasite refuses your death. Your restored life turns black; no healing until death.
curse.annihilation.status: Curse: %1$sm %2$ss until rescue is ready · Runes %3$s%% · %4$s
guidance.immortal_cultivation_mod.chapte: The Unfinished Curse
Learn the requirements, controls, and limits of the unfinished curse.
The Sealed Cradle

A swaddled newborn rests inside the Sealed Cradle Bottle. Breaking it yields no item: 480 black seals scatter, then slowly swarm the nearest living player in that dimension. They creep over the ground to the feet, crawl over the actual legs and torso, gather at the chest, then sink inside. Travel takes four to twenty seconds depending on distance; only completed entry grants One Whom Annihilation Has Not Finished. Contact infection does not copy this innate ability. The bottle currently comes from Creative inventory or /give @s immortal_cultivation_mod:sealed_cradle_bottle; it has no natural generation.
A Borrowed Life

At five percent HP, or when a hit would cross that threshold, the host is restored to full health once in that life. Restored HP appears black in both the mod health bar and AsteorBar and is spent first. The host cannot heal again until death. The thirty-minute cooldown advances only while online, survives death and reconnecting, and cannot be bypassed with another bottle.
Ink Beneath the Skin

After rescue, black runes creep from the chest across the host over eight seconds without harming it. They coat the base skin and visible outer hat, jacket, sleeve and trouser layers, including first-person sleeves. Each rune drifts independently, rebounds at model edges and bumps away from other runes; transparent skin pixels remain clear. Once the bloom finishes, accepted attacks plant runes; repeated hits accelerate growth. Infected targets lose Qi each second. Base HP corrosion is 1% of their maximum HP per second at full rune coverage, scaled down for partial coverage; defenses still apply. They cannot heal until death. Their saved coverage remains independent of the caster and survives departure or chunk unloading. Host death clears its own marks; infected players retain their target coverage on respawn.
Contact and Restraint

Touching an infected entity spreads runes, capped at half its current coverage. Repeated touches do not add another half. Full coverage can pass at most fifty percent; that recipient can pass at most twenty-five percent. Contact does not grant the rescue ability. Creative and spectator players are protected.
Meditation Against the Curse

Runes never expire on their own. Every full minute spent meditating removes one percentage point. Meditation pauses growth but grants neither cultivation progress nor method proficiency until all runes are gone. Remaining runes can resume growth after meditation stops. Full cleansing restores meditation experience; an existing healing lock still lasts until death.
When Domains Collide

At 200% release, a bright membrane marks your moving twenty-block domain. Hostile fields compress against one another; both membranes shudder and rebound as sparks, opposing streams and pressure waves erupt along their contact seam. Domain effects remain within the compressed boundary. After four seconds, the active method with the higher cultivation ceiling wins. Equal ceilings compare method proficiency; exact ties remain locked until separation or a changed advantage. The losing domain shatters while body Qi remains. Reopening requires three seconds of recovery. Players and NPCs follow the same rules.
message.immortal_cultivation_mod.qi_rele: Your domain shattered. Body Qi remains; recover for three seconds before reopening.
Domain recovering. Reopening requires three seconds after it shatters.
Golden Core or higher: hover in the air and fly to elevated targets or controller destinations. Enable movement to pursue. Finite Qi uses normal flight upkeep.
Remove harmful status effects, burns, bindings, domain freeze and marks, and Shentong curses. Active sources can apply them again. Keeps buffs, health, Qi and cooldowns.
Shift-right-click dummy to bind. Right-click a creature to select its target. Right-click a block to walk there; Shift-right-click to teleport. Right-click air for controls.
Toggle + to learn or forget. Casting obeys realm, method, Qi, target, range and cooldown rules. Healing and utility spells need their normal conditions.
Action blocked: check stats, knowledge, target, Qi and cooldown.
Shift-right-click a dummy to bind; left-click or right-click creatures to target; right-click air for controls.
Only its owner or an operator can control this dummy.
Bound dummy must be loaded, in the same dimension and within 96 blocks.
Domain needs Golden Core or higher, an active learned method, and freedom from full freezing.
Cannot cast: check knowledge, realm, method, target, range, Qi and cooldown.
Creative, spectator and protected targets cannot be selected.
Use a Dummy Control Stick to configure this dummy.
guidance.immortal_cultivation_mod.chapte: Training and Control

Get a Training Dummy and Dummy Control Stick from the creative inventory or /give. Place the dummy, then Shift-right-click it with the stick to bind. Right-click air for controls. Edit realm, maximum HP/Qi, physical/spell attack, armor and speed; choose exact learned methods and spells, method proficiency and active method. Golden Core or higher can open a real domain; passive effects need 500 proficiency and obey domain clashes. Spells keep their normal realm, method, target, Qi and cooldown rules. Left-click or right-click a creature to set the practice opponent. Selection causes no damage: NPCs and neutral mobs target the bound dummy, not the controller. Right-click a block to walk there, or Shift-right-click a block to teleport. Prevent death and unlimited Qi start enabled but can be disabled. Reset restores vitals, cooldowns and status. Binding survives saves. Only the owner or an operator holding the bound stick can control a loaded dummy in the same dimension within 96 blocks.
screen.immortal_cultivation_mod.method_s: Click to activate. Right-click or double-click to read.
guidance.immortal_cultivation_mod.chapte: Switch Methods

Click a learned method at the bottom of spell selection to activate it without closing the screen. A green border and check mark identify the active method. Use the arrows or scroll over the method area to reach more learned methods. Right-click or double-click a name to read its description and return. Switching preserves each method's proficiency and your spell-wheel order; active aura and domain follow the new method. Unlearned methods are not listed.
life.balance.encounter_insight: Encounter insight adds 5% of this realm's full cultivation requirement, capped at full progress.
life.expansion.routine.conditions_help: Unmet conditions skip this slot without spending actions. Below 30% health or above 85 strain, eligible activities become rest.
life.full_rewrite.life_story_ninth_sprin: Lu Shan gave you a bed last night. After breakfast, he asks whether you can take a parcel to the workshop across Apricot Bridge. Inside is a red-handled awl, worn pale where it was held. It looks nothing like a valuable spiritual tool.
Shan: “It belonged to our mother. My sister took it when she apprenticed herself to Yu Zhen, but he confiscated it. I found it among the belongings returned after his death.”
You: “Hasn't she come home for it?”
Shan: “She has stayed nearby since he expelled her last winter. He's been buried six weeks, but she says there's still a lesson he owes her.”
An old voice drifts from the chimney across the bridge. After a pause, it repeats the same cadence. Shan's face tightens at the sound.
Shan: “It's a recording, not someone still alive. Mei knows that. After eight years of waiting, she keeps thinking there's something in it she hasn't understood.”
You: “Do you want me to persuade her to return?”

Shan: “Ask whether she wants to, then bring me her own answer. Don't pressure her for me, and don't promise her a spirit root. Yu promised that for eight years. This is the ninth spring he told her to wait for.”
Mei sits outside the workshop with numbered wooden models beside her. You explain your errand and hand over the parcel. Recognizing the red handle, she runs her thumb across its pale worn patch.
Mei: “I thought he'd thrown it away. He said using mortal tools would leave me with mortal habits.”
You: “What did you make with it?”
Mei: “Hinges and stove doors. Things people used. After coming here, I somehow became ashamed to mention them.”
She lays the awl beside a model. The chimney recording sounds, and she looks toward the furnace almost automatically.
Mei: “I have no spirit root. That was tested. My master said the furnace could make one and told me to wait nine years. Last winter he expelled me without explaining. Then he died.”
You: “Do you want to keep trying?”
Mei: “I want to know what he actually achieved. If he failed, show me the records. I've heard enough people simply call me a fool.”
You: “Then we'll inspect the equipment and records. Show us the parts you know.”
Steward Shen Qiu inventories what the sect is reclaiming: the furnace core, experiment ledger and eleven tools. At the bottom, Mei's name appears beside “furnace attendant, unpaid.”
Shen: “I performed the test eight years ago. She had no spirit root. I gave Yu the result then.”
You: “Did she receive a copy herself?”
Shen checks the register but finds no receipt from her. He notes the omission without defending the procedure.
You: “Why hasn't the core been removed?”
Shen: “Heat remains trapped inside, and the shell is cracked. Moving it directly could burn the street. I can stabilize it, but its concealed pipe routes need the person who installed them.”
You: “Who was that?”
Shen: “Qin He, the landlord. Mei handled daily operations. Their knowledge doesn't become mine because my realm is higher.”

Someone waits at the gate with a tile invoice. Shen asks them to wait and confirms that inspection and safe removal are the sect's responsibility. Wages and negligence must be investigated separately.
Qin scrapes soot from a ceramic sleeve with a piece of wood. She owns the courtyard and installed Yu's furnace pipes. At your question, she turns the sleeve to expose its scorched outer surface.
Qin: “Heat came back along the outside toward the seat. Ordinary firing wouldn't leave this pattern.”
You: “Can you map the whole system?”
Qin: “Yes, with an afternoon's inspection. I have tiles to fire today. If I stay here, I miss the delivery.”
A worker is available to take over the firing for six stones. Qin can inspect without that payment, but the lost order must be acknowledged as a real cost.
Fresh scratches mark the storeroom gate, with a red scale beside them. Qin points toward a pile of hot stones and warns you not to reach in.
Qin: “Looks like an iron-scaled scorpion. The tool chest is on the platform beside it. Retrieving that will take a separate plan.”
You: “Could we inspect only the external controls?”
Qin: “Yes, but I won't draw unexamined pipes and let you think the map is complete.”
When the inspection begins, the awl her brother entrusted to you is beside Mei. She opens the ledger and places the measuring cup as usual, but does not sit in the chair before the furnace.
As the cooling valve turns, the recording disc repeats a lesson Yu recorded while alive.
Yu's recording: “Place your hand over the cup. A darkening copper ring means the spiritual seed has begun to awaken.”
Mei keeps both hands at her sides. The ring darkens anyway. Qin waits for it to cool, asks everyone to stand farther away, and repeats the test.
Qin: “It changes with the water temperature, not your hand.”
Mei: “I sat there for hours each time. He said moving would ruin everything.”
The final ledger pages record the same result: an empty chair, with the ring changing normally. Mei draws the book toward herself and asks to finish reading it first.
Qin: “The maintenance note is useful. The recording's last word marks a cooling interval for the gate. A complete pipe map could identify the interval without it.”
Mei: “If we keep it, only until the chest is dealt with. I don't want to hear him every time I open the door.”
Once Shen has joined them, Mei asks everyone to check the date. Yu recorded the empty-chair failure fourteen months before expelling her.
Mei: “For those fourteen months, he still told me to come every day.”
You read the next passage. The workshop depended on her, so he had asked her to wait another spring. By the end, Yu admits that needing an assistant became his excuse to keep promising.
Mei: “Was he going to show me, or was writing it enough to make him feel better?”
You: “He doesn't say. I can't supply an intention for him.”
Shen: “This furnace did not create a spirit root. The records contain no successful method that he simply withheld from you.”
Mei: “Even if someone of a higher realm came?”
Shen: “I know no method that would give you one. What I can establish is that these records do not support his promise.”
Mei closes the book. After a while, she asks what she can keep. Shen explains that ordinary fittings and hand tools belong to her, while the heat-laden core remains sect property.
Mei: “Separate them that way, then. I can't think through the rest of my life today. I can begin with what's here.”
Shan comes across the bridge with Mei's old bedding. It has been aired but not tied into luggage urging her to leave. He lays it on a bench and waits for her to speak.
Mei: “The furnace didn't work. He knew, and kept me tending it anyway.”
Shan: “Keep the ledger. If someone later says you simply failed to learn, show them.”
Mei: “You sent food for eight years.”
Shan: “You needed to eat. The rice wasn't wasted. It wasn't those sacks that kept you waiting.”
She grips the edge of the quilt and stops before speaking again. Shan leaves the book in her lap and sits at the other end of the bench.
Mei: “Giving up the workshop feels like admitting there was nothing in those eight years.”
You: “The models you built and repairs you made still count. You can decide whether to stay according to what you want to do now.”
Shan: “Coming home doesn't require an achievement. I didn't keep your bed waiting only for someone who could fly.”
Mei: “Make the furnace safe first. Then I'll think properly.”

A ceramic crack sounds inside the furnace room. Shen clamps the chamber with the prepared brace, stabilizing the new split while ordering everyone away from the hot wall. Qin checks the external gate and goes pale.
Qin: “One corner of the storeroom platform has burned through. The chest will fall with it.”
Mei: “My models are in there too.”
Shen: “Clear the street first. I'll hold this. Nobody enters the heated area.”
A red pincer scrapes beneath the gate. Qin identifies an iron-scaled scorpion and moves the nearest onlookers behind the wall.
Mei: “Could someone hold that for you while you retrieve the chest?”
Shen: “They need the realm and a practiced barrier technique compatible with the brace. I must confirm it will hold before changing hands.”
Qin: “The other route is operating the gate and winch from outside. If neither works, we seal the room and protect people.”
Mei: “Please see whether retrieval is possible. I want my belongings, not someone dying in there for them.”

The winch rope still reaches the chest, but the scorpion moves beneath the platform. Pulling directly could bring the platform down. Qin indicates a second gate: lowering that partition will lock the supports first.
Qin: “It jams under load. We need the cooling interval.”
You: “How do we know when it arrives?”
Mei: “The complete pipe map identifies an indicator. If the recording remains, its final word marks it too, as the maintenance note confirmed.”
Qin: “Once the partition drops, I can winch the chest from here. Nobody needs to climb onto it.”
The scorpion's tail strikes the stone wall. Mei steps back but keeps the indicator in view.
Mei: “Say which control you're using. I'll call the sequence. Don't start pulling things because it makes a noise.”

Qin points out the emergency gate as well. Immediate isolation protects those outside but sacrifices the platform and chest. Without reliable timing, fighting to clear the platform remains possible, at a different risk.

The cool-side doorway remains open behind you. As you approach through it, the scorpion turns, scoring the floor with a pincer. Qin holds the outside winch while Mei watches the heated tiles from behind the wall.
Mei: “Stay off the row on your right. Call when the platform is clear. We'll pull from outside.”
You: “Nobody needs to carry the chest out?”
Qin: “No. The rope is intact. Concentrate on what's in front of you.”
Still at the core, Shen calls through the wall: withdraw if you cannot hold it off. Retrieving the chest must not become a rescue of you.
Mei grips her mother's awl, then puts it back in her pocket instead of attempting to fight with it.
Mei: “I'll call positions from here. If you retreat, I'll help Qin seal the gate. I won't run inside.”
The tail rises. The route back through the cool-side door is still clear.
With the storeroom dealt with, Shen still cannot release the brace. Qin writes down three ways to handle the furnace. Mei asks what each would preserve and what it would cost.
Shen: “Transfer the equipment and research to the sect. Separately, I can offer a year's paid work as an instrument assistant. You decide whether to accept.”
Qin: “With the complete map and recovered gauges, we can safely deactivate the core, retain the ordinary shell, and fit a wood firebox for a repair shop.”
Mei: “And complete destruction?”
Shen: “Destroy the core and main research. The ordinary shell won't survive either. Keep the failure and safety records so the same thing isn't sold as a method again.”
You: “Can she postpone all three?”
Shen: “Yes. Secure and guard it, then arrange removal. Her belongings and losses will be recorded separately from sect property.”
Mei asks Qin to erase any remaining recording. The chimney falls silent. She watches it for a while before returning to the paper.
Mei: “The tools survived. I want to see what I can make with them. This time, begin with something achievable.”
Mei: “I know sealing the room protected people. Losing the chest still hurts. You don't have to talk me out of that yet.”
Shen draws up an employment contract rather than adding Mei to a disciple register. Sitting opposite him, she asks about pay, instruction and how she could leave.
Mei: “Pay begins on the first day. No saying that someone learning should work for nothing.”
Shen: “From the first day. Instruction covers measurement and instrument repair, not cultivation methods.”
Mei: “I see the failed trials too, and nobody uses me to test the furnace.”
Shen: “Access to the complete records under supervision. No further human trials with this furnace. That goes in the safety terms.”
You: “What happens to her work after the year?”
Shen: “Private models remain hers; employed research belongs to the sect. She may leave at the end without waiting for another unspecified spring.”
After reading it, Mei asks whether refusing the job would affect her belongings. Shen confirms that transfer and employment are separate. Recovering her property does not require accepting the post.
Mei: “Then this is a choice I can actually make.”
The complete map lies beside the recovered gauges. Qin draws a chalk line around the ordinary shell. Shen confirms that the heat-laden core is excluded before agreeing to the dismantling sequence.
Qin: “Keep the shell and fit a wood firebox. It will warm the bench, not create a root. We'll say that from the first day.”
Mei: “I'd like to begin with hinges. Ones that don't catch sleeves or need a kick to open.”
Qin: “People will buy those. I can rent you a bench. Let's agree on rent and term before work begins.”
Mei: “I won't be able to pay until I've completed three paid repairs.”
Qin: “Then rent begins after the third. If you leave later, settle the agreed account. An apprenticeship title won't bind you here.”
Mei: “I can't repay the order you lost mapping this. I can help with the next batch for ten afternoons. If you agree, write that separately from rent.”
Qin: “Agreed. Ten afternoons settles that promise. You won't owe me for everything afterward.”
You can commit two afternoons, pay for a worker, or simply witness their own arrangements. Shen remains at the brace until the plan is confirmed.

Mei separates the final failure records and asks Shen about retaining a certified copy when the core is destroyed. Hearing that the furnace may be shut down, Shan comes to stay with her without urging a decision.
Mei: “Keep these so someone can check later. I don't want to be blamed for leaving one step before success because I couldn't wait.”
Shen: “We can establish this device's failure, not declare that nobody anywhere could ever succeed. The report will state what was verified.”
You: “Destroying the remaining research and shell means they cannot become a workshop.”
Mei: “I understand. I'm still finding it hard to let go, though I know it isn't the cup I want to keep.”
Shan: “You don't need a respectable explanation for finding it hard. Take your time. We're here.”
Shen has Qin check the street again while he holds the brace. Once destruction begins, nobody may reenter for a final trial. Until the order is given, Mei can still choose storage.
Mei puts the awl in her pocket. “Don't publish every private detail about me. Let me decide how much is disclosed too.”
The equipment is secured under sect guard pending safe removal. Qin records completed and unfinished work separately, along with the belongings actually recovered and those lost.
Shan: “Where is Mei staying tonight?”
Mei: “Home. Tonight. Don't tell the whole village I've decided the rest of my life.”
Shan: “All right. Tonight is all I'll say.”
She asks about the ledger. Shen confirms that it remains sealed in sect custody, with her right to inspect it written on the receipt. Temporary safekeeping has not become a donation.
Qin: “Look after anyone injured first. People can authorize testimony when they're conscious. There's no need to force it now.”
Mei: “I'd like to think before writing mine too. Enough people have spoken for me these eight years.”
There is space for a signed complaint, and an option to report privately to the family. Neither choice withdraws evidence independently provided by others.
Once the stored heat is controlled, trained workers remove the furnace. Mei checks equipment and private belongings against the inventory before the last cart leaves. The recording has been erased.
There is no root-testing chair at her new bench. On her first day, Shen gives her a valve and asks what she would do if it opened before the handle moved.
Mei: “Stop and find the unintended connection. Don't keep forcing it just to finish the trial.”
Shen: “Keep the record too. Repairing it doesn't remove the need to know what failed.”
Mei: “Even if the whole device turns out to be useless?”
Shen: “Especially then.”
She earns her first wages as a mortal and takes on the year's contractual duties. Her lessons concern measurement and repair. Nobody calls a payslip a promise of a new spirit root.
Mei stands beside Shan as the last cart crosses the bridge. The equipment leaves without her.
Shan: “What should I say when people ask what you'll do next?”
Mei: “Tell them to ask me. I may not have an answer yet, but it should be mine.”
Shan: “Let's go home for a meal first.”
Refusing the job costs her none of her private property and supplies no ready-made livelihood. She puts away the inventory and crosses with her brother, beginning with what she can decide today.
The wood firebox warms the repair bench. Mei marks holes with the red-handled awl, fits a hinge to a customer's door panel and asks him to test it himself.
Customer: “That is easier. Can you make a matching pair?”
Mei: “Yes. We'll measure first and agree on the price.”
Qin records the order, keeping wages and rent in separate columns. Mei checks the figures before accepting the next repair.
Mei: “Record my ten afternoons helping with tiles separately. I know they can't restore the lost order.”
Qin: “Helping with the next batch completes that agreement. Don't turn it into a lifetime debt.”
Qin: “The tiles were delivered on time. You don't owe work for a loss I didn't suffer.”
Mei: “Then we'll record the account we actually have.”

The new sign offers repairs and basic woodwork lessons, with details discussed in person. Mei does not put Yu's name above the door, nor erase everything she learned during those eight years. She begins by teaching a hinge that will not catch a sleeve.

The core is destroyed and the furnace shut down as planned. The main research goes with it, and the ordinary shell is unusable. The surviving report records the specific failure, with disclosure limited to what Mei agreed.
Outside the sealed courtyard, Mei asks her brother whether she ought to feel relieved.
Shan: “You don't have to feel relieved yet. You haven't eaten properly all day. Let's go home first.”
Shen hands her the safety receipt. “This records what was done to the equipment. It doesn't tell you how to feel about the eight years.”
Mei: “Don't write that I've stopped wanting to learn either. I've stopped waiting for this furnace.”
Qin helps check the private belongings recovered, without pretending destroyed models are in the parcel. The red-handled awl remains in Mei's pocket.
At the bridge, Shan asks what to tell people at home. Mei says to begin with what she agreed to disclose. The rest can wait until she wants to talk.
Qin's later account contains no miracle. The equipment remains sealed under sect guard. Mei is staying with her brother, without accepting a new job or restarting the dangerous lesson.
Shan: “Yesterday she asked where to buy a plane for repairing woodwork.”
Qin: “Did you buy one for her?”
Shan: “No. I asked whether she wanted company. She said she'd like to choose it herself.”
Mei later visits Qin's bench and measures it without immediately agreeing to rent. The receipt still grants access to the experiment ledger. For now she does not use it.
Mei: “I used to wake afraid of being late. I'm not used to nobody waiting to scold me.”
Qin: “Give it a few days. Being undecided isn't another failure to record.”

Signed complaints are submitted only as actually authorized; private reports remain with the family. Nobody invents conversations for an unconscious or deceased witness. Losses and surviving evidence are recorded as they stand.
For three nights you have been lodging at Reedbank's clinic, carrying water by day and sleeping behind the medicine cabinet. Tonight Du Fen has just served your rice when the village bell rings. At the third stroke, she stops with the soup still in her hands.
Du: “There should only be two strokes at this hour. Qiao took the bell rope down to inspect it yesterday. He hasn't put it back.”
You: “Is he still at the sluice?”
She sets down the soup and looks outside, but coughing from the ward brings her back.
Du: “He went at dawn. This afternoon someone from the sect said he'd blocked a drain and was wanted for questioning. They wouldn't tell me whether they'd found him.”
You: “You want me to look for him?”

Du: “And find out what's happened to the sluice. Six people here vomit whenever they drink from the well. I can't leave them. If you go, bring me word before the third sunrise, whether you've managed anything or not.”
You: “Even if he really did block it?”
Du: “I want him alive to explain himself. I can't answer for what he's done.”
She takes paper from the medicine cabinet and writes a short message. First she asks her son to come home. Then she adds that his boots are dry and waiting beside the stove.

Tao Wen is removing a cover from the mill axle. When you mention Du Fen, he sets his tools aside and brings a cup from the windowsill. Black particles lie at the bottom, with a small magnet resting across the rim.
Tao: “From the well. People blame my millstones. Try the magnet.”
The particles follow it. He lets you see that before continuing.
You: “Iron filings. Has Qiao seen this?”
Tao: “He brought the magnet. He suspected the channel that bypasses our measuring weir, then nailed its lower outlet shut. The water rose, all right. The well got worse too.”
You: “Why bypass the measuring weir?”
He unfolds a copied order: one additional withdrawal daily, for ten days. Beside the accountant Ren Bo's seal is Du Fen's mark.
Tao: “Ask the sect about that. First, the old bridge won't hold much longer, and I can't shore it up alone.”
You: “How long would it take?”
Tao: “Half a day with your help. Twelve stones would hire three workers and save time. Or try the sect checkpoint at the main entrance. I can't promise they'll let us through.”

A checkpoint stands at the ruined shrine, but nobody inside has a comfortable place to sit. Steward Xu Lan kneels beside a bronze pressure regulator, holding a crack together. Tao introduces himself as the village observer and leads you onto dry ground.
Xu: “Speak from there. It's slippery here, and I haven't a hand free to catch you.”
You: “You're holding the regulator together?”
Xu: “For nearly two hours. Before you ask why I haven't stopped the water, look at the return-pressure pipe.”
The pipe trembles under the strain. Closing the upstream gate first, he explains, would trap the pressure in the regulator. If it bursts, the surge will reach the village.
You: “Someone must know how to stop it.”
Xu: “Qiao does. He's tended it for years. But Ren says he damaged it, and Qiao won't come out. I haven't heard his account.”
Tao: “Let us through, then. You might get it.”
Xu has an attendant pass you a sealed inspection permit.
Xu: “It covers the accounts and the lower valve. If there's immediate danger, I authorize an emergency shutdown. Arrests and judgments are separate. Don't promise those on my behalf.”

Muddy water runs beneath the old bridge. Across it, the records room leans at an angle. A red ledger remains on a shelf, with the water barely a hand below it. Tao tests the bridgehead without stepping onto it.
Tao: “Qiao recorded every withdrawal. Lose that book, and we'll have only Ren's figures to go on.”
Before you can ask where Qiao is, an answer comes from behind the wall below.
Qiao: “I'm at the lower valve! Don't come through the room. The floor's gone underneath!”
Tao: “Why didn't you call out sooner?”
Qiao: “I shouted and knocked on the pipe. You couldn't hear over the water. The moment I let go, this lever springs back.”
You: “There may be time for the ledger. Can you hold on?”
Qiao: “I can't tell you how long. And mind the boards to the right of the shelf. They look solid, but they're broken underneath.”
Tao points out the narrow surviving ledge, then the watercourse leading to Qiao.
Tao: “The bridge is usable if we braced it. A suitable movement technique could get you across too. Otherwise you'd have to judge that ledge carefully. We can reach Qiao without crossing it.”
Ren Bo keeps his document chest raised on two bricks beside the inspection table. After examining the permit, he moves aside, then asks which area you intend to inspect first.
You: “You know where Qiao is. Why tell people he can't be found?”
Ren: “I said he wouldn't come out for questioning.”
Tao: “With both hands holding the valve, how would he?”
Ren does not answer that. Instead, he takes the ten-day emergency order from his chest.
Ren: “The extra water went to workshops downstream. The proceeds supported twenty-three patients at the mountain infirmary. Nine came from this village.”
You: “Have the ten days passed?”
Ren: “They have.”
You: “Then why show me this order?”
His hand rests on the lid. Behind him, timber cracks in the records room, and he looks up.
Ren: “The later withdrawals are in the red ledger. You can still fetch it now. Go to Qiao first if you prefer, but I can't promise the shelf will survive until you return.”

The ledger's edges are wet, but most entries remain legible. Tao lays it somewhere dry and checks the dates. For forty-two days, an extra withdrawal appears beside a buyer's name and Ren's authorization.
Tao: “Du approved the first ten days. For the next thirty-two, he never asked the village.”
You: “The income matches the infirmary's expenses. The maintenance money went there too.”
Tao: “That explains the missing replacement sleeve. I thought something had happened on the road.”
You: “He may not have pocketed it, but it wasn't his maintenance fund to spend.”
Tao finds paper and charcoal and signs his name in a corner.
Tao: “I'll testify to what we've read. Make two copies: one for you and one for the village. We shouldn't leave Ren holding the only record again.”
You: “Du's mark has to go in too.”
Tao: “Of course. I'd like her to speak for herself before she hears her own story from the whole street.”
You: “Once copies leave us, I can't control who talks. Keeping it private means sealing the original.”
Tao: “Say which you mean, then. I'll do that and give the same account later.”
Qiao stands barefoot beside the lower valve, his arms braced against its lever and red marks across his wrists. You read Du's message aloud. At the mention of his dry boots, he finally looks up.
Qiao: “Has she been giving you her own dinner again?”
You: “Dinner is still on the table. Tell me first why you nailed the drain shut.”
Qiao: “That channel bypassed the measuring weir. The village couldn't see how much they took. I wanted the water out in the open where they couldn't hide it.”
Tao: “Instead, it backed into the well.”
Qiao: “I know. By the time I understood, it was blocked and everything below was flooded. I couldn't risk letting go.”
He nods toward a dry iron box at his feet. Inside are the returned petition and the emergency order, their folds worn pale.
You: “You knew your mother signed the ten-day order?”
Qiao: “She asked me to give the infirmary ten days. I did. Afterward I sent two petitions. One came back, and they struck my wages off the roll.”
Qiao: “The nails are mine. Don't hide that. But submit these too. Don't let the record say only that I went mad and wrecked the sluice.”
Qiao: “My mother believed you'd get me heard before they took me in. I'd like to believe it too. Tell me to my face what you're going to do.”
Tao: “While we were bracing the bridge, the clinic used another barrel of clean water. Du sent someone to ask us to hurry. Nothing more.”

Xu hears Qiao's explanation across the low wall and agrees to a controlled test. Qiao asks Tao to watch the water level and you to relay instructions. Each movement waits for an answer from the other side.
Qiao: “Lower valve first, then loosen the nailed board. Steward Xu, if the regulator won't hold, call a stop immediately.”
Xu: “Understood. Slowly. Don't release it all at once.”
Water gradually drains through the channel. Tao sees black filings wash from the damaged valve sleeve, then traces the water-level arm to the bell tower's striker.
Tao: “At the third mark it strikes three times by itself. Only the hand rope was removed. The warning mechanism is still connected!”
As the level falls, the well stops flooding and the striker returns to rest. Qiao inserts the locking pin and can finally take his arms off the lever.
Qiao: “Blocking the drain was wrong. I admit it. But the old sleeve was shedding iron, and the extra withdrawals were real.”
Xu: “I've seen it. We've only stopped the water temporarily. Restoring service requires a new sleeve.”
You: “How would you pay for it?”

Xu: “The toll reserve covers repairs, but then the infirmary needs support elsewhere. Willing owners could lease reed fields for medicinal crops for four summers. That income would support it. If neither works, we must disconnect the watercourses permanently.”
Two sect guards wait at the exit with their swords sheathed. Holding a custody order, Ren looks at Qiao's hands before checking his name.
Ren: “Come with us to Steward Xu. The guards will keep you in custody on the way. There will be no punishment before the hearing.”
Qiao: “You didn't wait for a hearing before striking off my wages.”
You: “Why didn't you forward his petitions?”
Ren: “They would have stopped the extra withdrawals. I knew how much the infirmary needed next month and had no way to replace it.”
Tao: “So you spent the replacement fund as well?”
Ren: “I thought the old sleeve would last. Delaying the replacement seemed better than turning patients away.”
Qiao: “You decided for everyone, then.”
Ren offers no answer. He has a guard unfold the order so you can record its date and promises.
Quietly, Tao tells you villagers are waiting outside. With the inspection permit or their trust, you could argue for a witnessed escort to the hearing instead of formal custody.
When you block the guards, they draw their swords. Tao pulls Qiao behind the stone partition. Ren retreats to the inspection table. Nobody touches the regulator's controls.
Ren: “Even if you win, don't damage the sluice. There are people behind that wall.”
You: “I want Qiao to walk to the hearing without being taken into custody.”
Guard: “Our orders are to hold him and deliver him. Stand down now and you can still accompany us.”
Qiao peers around the wall. Tao immediately pulls him back.
Qiao: “Don't ruin yourself over me. We can't help you in a fight.”
Ren: “Accept registered custody, and I'll put your right to accompany him in writing. That offer still stands.”
The guards take separate positions across the passage and wait for your decision. Water roars behind the wall, drowning out everyone else's breathing.
Tao opens the outer door. Villagers enter carrying empty buckets. One woman leaves her child by the entrance, approaches Ren, and sets her bucket on the dry stone floor.
Woman: “We came for water, and to accompany Qiao. Wherever you take him, we'll see him there.”
Ren: “This isn't a place for a crowd to start a quarrel.”
Woman: “Then speak to us properly. Nobody's brought a weapon.”
You explain that witnessing this may mean putting their names on a petition. She gives hers and asks you to read the document aloud before submitting it.
Qiao: “Read all of mine too. Don't mention the petitions and leave out the blocked drain.”
Tao: “You can tell them yourself. We're listening.”
Ren looks at the empty buckets gathered by the door and finally folds away the custody order.
Ren: “Witnessed escort, then. At Steward Xu's, you can decide whether to speak publicly or seal the evidence while we discuss terms.”
You: “Nobody takes him aside on the way.”
Ren: “Put it in the record.”
Another healer takes over at the clinic so Du can come to the sluice. She touches Qiao's arm, checks that he can stand, and pushes the coat she has brought into his hands.
Qiao: “I blocked the drain.”
Du: “I'm listening. Don't rush to repeat everyone else's accusations as your own.”
You place the ten-day order before her and ask why she agreed to it.
Du: “The infirmary said they'd send our nine patients home without more income. I didn't even have empty beds. I thought ten days would give us time to find something.”
Xu: “And on the eleventh day? Did anyone ask you again?”
Du: “No. I asked Ren whether things were holding. He said they were. That was what I wanted to hear.”
Ren: “I kept authorizing the money. You can't put that all on her.”

Still holding the regulator, Xu asks everyone to discuss it here. He lays out the three routes: publicly fund repairs from the reserve and relocate the patients; support the infirmary through voluntary field leases; or close the sluice permanently.
Tao: “Being here today doesn't make an unwilling landowner a consenting one.”
Xu: “Of course. Each household signs for itself. I have no authority to do it for them.”
Qiao: “One more thing belongs in the record. You promised my mother a hearing first. I was taken into custody first instead. Don't call those the same thing.”
Qiao: “With Steward Xu listening, I'll sign my statement now. Include both the drain and the petitions.”
An upturned flour box serves as a table. Tao lays out the available evidence and has the witnesses name each item so that a missing document cannot pass unnoticed.
Tao: “Here's the ten-day order, and witnesses saw the valve test. If the withdrawal ledger survived, we'll check its dates alongside these.”
Du: “The mark is mine. My failure to follow up belongs in the account. Don't alter it for me.”
Qiao: “I admit blocking the drain and misjudging the backflow. The date my petition came back is there too. Please read it.”
Xu: “The testimony supports a temporary shutdown. A formal ruling on unauthorized withdrawals and compensation requires the ledger, order and test results to agree.”
You: “What happens first if the ruling is issued?”
Xu: “The reserve buys a sleeve. Ren loses withdrawal authority pending an audit. Without that subsidy, the infirmary must relocate its patients.”
Du: “I'll find beds. Don't write that they're already settled. I haven't even asked everywhere yet.”
Tao: “Compensation won't revive this season's seedlings either. Understand that before signing.”
Tao: “You promised to seal the original. If you disclose it today, I'll still testify to the facts, but the promise will have been broken.”

After visiting the households, Tao returns with six owners' consent. Their plots make up roughly half the village's reed fields. Unsigned land remains outside the marked boundaries, which Xu has copied afresh.
Tao: “Four summers only. Write the starting year and the return date plainly.”
Xu: “The sect guarantees grain rent even if the medicinal crop fails. That risk won't fall on the owners. Remaining income supports the infirmary, leaving the toll reserve for repairs.”
Ren: “There may be no profit in it for the sect.”
Tao: “We didn't profit from those forty-two days either.”
Qiao: “You've settled the land. What happens to me?”
Xu: “Paid maintenance work under supervision. Your responsibility for the drain stays in the sealed case. Unpaid wages remain a separate debt; new wages won't erase it.”
Du: “Can Ren still authorize withdrawals?”
Xu: “Only with oversight. His salary guarantees compliance, and the audit continues.”
Tao: “Two households demanded his dismissal and left when they heard that. Even the signers aren't all satisfied. They want water back on their fields.”
Qiao draws both watercourses on the stone, marking the inlets, lower valves and connecting rod. Xu checks each point until the workers can repeat the shutdown sequence themselves.
Qiao: “Close both ends before removing the connection. Nobody moves their part early because they're tired of waiting.”
You: “How will the village irrigate afterward?”
Tao: “The shared irrigation will be gone. Those who stay will repair rain cisterns. Some are already asking about work elsewhere.”
Xu: “Without buying the sleeve, the reserve goes toward moving all twenty-three patients. It won't be diverted again.”
Du: “I'll accompany our nine. I won't return until their new carers have received them.”
Qiao: “Rebuilding someday isn't impossible.”
Tao: “Then someday we'll find new money and ask every household again. Don't persuade people today as if this were only a few days without water.”
The workers lay their own tools on dry ground and await Xu's order. He asks you to relay messages or call valve positions, taking on only what you can actually manage.
Back at the clinic, the original bowl of rice has gone cold. Du moves it aside and spreads your papers on the table. Tao stays to add what he witnessed himself.
Du: “Qiao first. Where is he?”
Tao: “Under guard, awaiting what follows. I've recorded where he was taken and who took him.”
Tao: “With the witnesses, without being confined. The hearing still has to follow.”
Du nods and asks you to begin with your arrival at the sluice. At the news of the temporary shutdown, she covers the water jar and glances toward the ward.
Du: “Now that we know the cause, someone must follow it through. Tonight we still have to ration what we've got.”
You: “We couldn't reach an agreement.”
Du: “Then write that. If you were afraid, you can say so. Don't make unfinished work sound finished to comfort me.”
Tao: “A signed account will give the inspector something to follow up.”
Du: “You could stay a few days too. Tending the stove or carrying messages helps. If you're hurt, rest first.”

The workers arrive with the replacement sleeve. The village bell returns to one morning stroke and two in the evening. Dead seedlings still cover much of the fields. People stop to look as they pass; posting the ruling has not made them forget that loss.
Xu: “Both sides will sign every withdrawal. Petitions get a separate copy outside Ren's office.”
Qiao: “When can I go home?”
Xu: “Now. Your responsibility for the drain still needs investigation, and your maintenance work will be supervised. Filing petitions doesn't remove that.”
Du comes for her son carrying borrowed bedding. She has found only three beds and must keep arranging places for the remaining patients.
Du: “Put your boots on when you get home. Help where you can. No more disappearing into the water without a word.”
Qiao: “Next time I wait for an answer, I'll keep my own copy.”

You leave with a witness record. Limits and responsibility can now be traced, though each household must still endure the ruined harvest. Du keeps a bed for you; it is the thanks she can presently offer.
At the door Tao says, “I stand by the testimony. But next time you offer to keep something private for me, I'll have to think about it.”

When the first guaranteed grain arrives, the six landowning households count it together. The four-summer term begins with this advance. The boundary map and lease are stored together in the village's dry chest.
Tao: “They tried moving a boundary stake yesterday. I took the map over. This morning they moved it back.”
You: “So you'll have to keep watching.”
Tao: “Of course. A signature won't watch the fields for us.”
Qiao returns to the repaired sluice with a supervisor beside him. At every withdrawal, both check the level marks before signing.
Du: “All twenty-three patients kept their beds. Three households here now prefer the next village's healer. I can't stop them.”
You: “And Ren?”
Du: “Still working under oversight, with his salary held as security. Don't mistake that for forgiveness. People are trying to live under the agreement they've made.”

Before you leave, Du clears your lodging account. There is no celebration. Qiao only asks that on your next visit you look at the stakes and water level before accepting anyone's assurance that all is well.
Removing the final connecting rod nudges the striker, producing one short stroke. Qiao waits for the echo to fade before putting the closure papers in the dry chest.
Qiao: “Both sides are disconnected. Restoring water will mean rebuilding.”
Tao: “And asking each household again. An empty watercourse doesn't give anyone our fields.”
Du has confirmed the receiving infirmaries. The sect provides escorts, and she accompanies the village's nine patients, tying each name onto the proper medicine bundle before leaving.
You: “When will they return?”
Du: “Let them recover first. I won't set a date for them.”
At the entrance one household is loading a cart. Another asks Qiao to inspect its rain cistern. He retrieves his boots from the clinic and returns to help, leaving the old lever behind.

The sluice no longer binds the two sides together, and its irrigation is lost with it. Your report is delivered, but there is no repair bounty to collect. Tao walks you to the road, then turns back to help carry a cupboard.

For now, the sluice remains closed, compensation unsettled and the infirmary's transfers still being arranged. Tao writes those facts first, making sure an explanation of the cause does not conceal the unfinished work.
Du: “Write Qiao's part as it happened. Name whoever took him away, or whoever stayed with him.”
Tao: “The promises too?”
Du: “Yes. I can understand fear. I won't give a broken promise a kinder name.”

Tao completes the account of what he witnessed. Du keeps a copy; another is reserved for whoever continues the investigation. She does not call it enough and checks with Tao for any detail they may have missed.
For seven days you help at the clinic as your health permits. Du acknowledges that work while leaving “sluice unrepaired” in the report.
Your signed statement reaches the sect inspector's office. Tao brings back the receipt and reminds everyone that receipt is not a ruling.

Water must still be rationed, and responsibility still pursued. No additional reward is offered. When someone eventually asks, the clinic will have a signed account that does not place every fault on Qiao.
life.full_rewrite.life_story_winter_coat: Nineteen days after Stone-Lamp's kiln collapse, mourning cloth still hangs over the tailor's door. Duan He invites you inside, puts away the collar she is sewing, and takes a receipt from her account book. It names Jian Cheng as the recipient. The date is yesterday.
Duan: “Jian Cheng was my husband. I washed his face before we buried him.”
You: “Could someone else have the same name?”
She turns the receipt over and points to the address and the note: unable to provide a thumbprint. Jian lost his right thumb working at the kiln. Everyone in the village knew it.
Duan: “The office brought it yesterday to check whether the coat fitted. I've asked everyone I can. Nobody will tell me who received it.”
You: “Do you want the impersonation investigated, or the relief payment?”
Duan: “First find out who used his name. I can pursue a debt. They can't declare him dead and then bring him back whenever they need a signature.”
She places two spirit stones at the corner of the table as payment for an account of what happened.
Duan: “And tell me first when you find out. I don't want to be the last to hear, through people outside my shop.”

A delivery mark on the receipt leads you to a funeral cart outside the village. Its driver, Tang Qi, is wrapping six food bowls in a woolen cloth beneath an empty coffin. When he sees your paper, his hands slow.
Tang: “Who sent you?”
You: “Duan. She wants to know where the coats collected in her husband's name went.”
He sighs and folds back the cloth he has just tucked in.
Tang: “Six people in the old drying house escaped the collapse. The register says they're dead, so they can't collect meals. I've been bringing food on the funeral cart.”
You: “Who changed the register?”
Tang: “Gu Tang. Ask him to explain his reasons himself. I can tell you this: of those seven names, Jian was the only person I buried.”

He pats the cart shaft. His sister has two empty rooms across the river and will take all six. Tomorrow's passage is booked, but their tools must be loaded before sunset to avoid extra freight charges.
You: “You're planning to take them away.”
Tang: “If they want to go. We still need to establish whether they can leave lawfully.”
People waiting for wages crowd Steward Pei Xun's desk. When your turn comes, he studies the receipt, then points to a small hook at the end of the signature.
Pei: “Gu's handwriting. We used to copy accounts together. I recognize it.”
You: “So you knew someone was collecting coats under a dead man's name?”
Pei: “I knew the records were wrong. Seven death reports, but only Jian's body was accounted for. That's why a hundred and forty spirit stones are being held.”
You: “Who is owed that money?”
Pei: “Twenty in wages for each of the six, and twenty in death relief for Duan. Finding it doesn't make it a reward for the investigator.”
He produces an inspection warrant and marks the damaged records room. Jian's shift order remains there. Tang knows the safe approach and can guide you.
You: “Won't you come and see them?”
Pei looks at the queue. “If these families leave unpaid today, they'll have to come back tomorrow. I'll finish here and join you.”
Washed bandages dry outside the old drying house. Gu returns from delivering broth and recognizes the receipt. He does not make you argue about the signature.
Gu: “I signed it. All six coats were collected under Jian's name.”
You: “Did you take Duan's relief money too?”
Gu: “No. They were surplus coats. Jian remained on the relief list. Restoring the other six as living workers would have brought new work orders.”
You: “Even with their injuries?”
Gu: “Supervisor Mu said anyone able to stand could sort ore. They refused, and I argued. In the end I reported seven bodies, hoping to get them through the immediate pressure.”
You: “Did they agree to that report?”
Gu: “They said they didn't want to return. I chose what to write. Don't make that their decision.”
He opens the issue ledger and asks Tang to check where each coat went. Someone coughs in the side room. Gu listens but remains seated.
Gu: “Copy it now if you need a record. I'll sign it. Then please see them too, rather than only my false paperwork.”

Tang takes you outside the records room and points through the broken wall to a sheet pinned under tiles. Its circled instruction remains legible: do not open the vent until the sixth cart is full. Supervisor Mu's seal sits below it.
Tang: “Jian kept that copy. He used to say a supervisor could forget a spoken order by the next day.”
You: “How can we reach it?”
Tang: “Don't go inside. That beam has split through. We can brace it from outside with timber from my cart and dismantle it slowly. Half a day should do.”
You look at the light. Half a day would cost them the free freight space for their tools.
Tang: “I know. We can find another way for the tools. Sending someone under that beam isn't worth it.”
You: “What about retrieving it from outside with a technique?”
Tang: “If you already know how and can avoid the supports, yes. This isn't the place to teach yourself.”
He unloads rope and timber and waits for your decision.

Six people sit in the drying house. Some mend sacks; others hold bowls and wait for the broth to cool. Shao Ning's right hand is splinted. He tries moving a stool for you, then asks a companion to help.
Shao: “Did Gu tell you we were dead or alive?”
You: “He said you refused to sort ore again.”
Shao: “I can't close this hand. They looked at it and said an outer disciple should endure more than a mortal. I learned swordwork, not how to carry things with broken fingers.”
You: “Was Jian with you?”
Shao: “The door jammed. He held it so we could get out. When I went back for him, he was dying. I took him to Tang. I couldn't bring myself to face Duan afterward.”
You: “And kept borrowing his name.”
Shao: “We told ourselves the coats were spare, that nobody would lose one. We didn't think about how the receipt would feel in her hands.”
Asked about testifying, he says he will speak publicly if the sealed shift order is recovered. Without it, he will speak privately to Pei. The other five must decide for themselves.
Shao insists on accompanying you to the tailor's. Duan listens without sitting, then brings soft lining cloth and lays it beside his uninjured left hand.
Duan: “That wool scratches. Have someone sew this inside so it doesn't rub your wounds.”
Shao: “You still want to help us?”
Duan: “I didn't say I wasn't angry. The cloth can help. Your wounds don't need to suffer for it.”
Shao: “I was afraid you'd ask why I got out when he didn't.”
Duan: “I want to know whether he realized the roof was coming down.”
Shao: “No. He kept waiting for someone to open the vent and cursed the supervisor for being deaf.”
Duan lowers her head and smooths a crease from the lining.
Duan: “He told me he was frightened of that roof. When you speak of him, don't make him someone who never felt fear. He wanted to come home too.”
Shao: “I will.”
She pushes the agreed two stones toward you, then says she wants to hear Pei's answer as well.
Everyone meets at the old drying house. Pei arrives alone and reaches to examine Shao's hand. Shao rests the splint on the table instead, leaving Pei to look across it.
Shao: “You saw it before you signed the new assignment.”
Pei: “I asked whether you could hold a brush.”
Shao: “Then write down what you asked and what work you assigned afterward.”
Pei writes it down without asking for a more respectful tone.
You: “What can be done now?”
Pei: “Suspend the assignments. A formal case would close the mine for inspection, interrupting income for thirty households. If evidence is missing, I can't pretend otherwise.”
Gu: “And without a public case?”
Pei: “A settlement releases the hundred and forty stones and provides six months' lodging plus suitable paid work. It requires waiving further accident claims. I need to say that first.”
Tang: “They could also choose to cross the river. Two rooms are available. Work isn't promised.”
Pei: “Before formal custody, I can authorize departure. Gu's false report remains a separate matter. Their leaving won't erase it.”
Pei goes to register the hearing, but two officers reach the drying house first with a custody order. They read the six names from their list, omitting nobody.
You: “They have just given their account to Steward Pei.”
Officer: “Our order concerns false deaths and identity claims. With an inspection warrant and signed individual statements, we can use voluntary escort. Otherwise we register custody first.”
Gu: “I wrote the report. Why take them first?”
Officer: “The author must be investigated, and the people named must be identified.”
Shao: “We're sitting here, showing you our names and injuries. What else do you need?”
The officer lays out the order so you can read the voluntary-escort conditions. His hand has not moved to his sword.
Tang leads the other five behind the partition and asks Shao to join them.
Tang: “Decide now whether to object or produce the papers. Don't leave them in the doorway to shield anyone from a sword.”
The officers draw their swords when you block the exit. Tang sends the injured workers inside and stays by the door, pointing toward the empty stone yard.
Tang: “Take it outside. This roof survived. Don't cost them their last shelter as well.”
Officer: “Stand aside and there's no fight. We're taking them to a hearing, not an execution ground.”
You: “Custody and voluntary attendance aren't the same thing.”
Officer: “Then you should produce the documents authorizing voluntary attendance.”
Both sides move onto the paving. The officers keep close enough to support one another, without rushing into the shelter.
From the doorway Shao calls, “We're arguing about how we go, not who survives to go. If you stand down, we can keep speaking for ourselves.”
You can still accept registered custody. Continuing means fighting with the abilities you actually possess. The injured workers cannot make up any shortfall.

The hearing takes place under the tailor's long eaves. Duan has the cloth moved aside and asks the crowd to make room for the injured workers to sit. Pei begins by requiring a record of who testifies and what each actually says.
Gu unfolds the sealed order. At “until the sixth cart is full,” Shao looks up.
Shao: “The third cart wasn't even full. Jian had asked twice for the vent to be opened.”
Pei: “I signed the reassignment after the collapse. Record that too.”
Duan: “Don't record only the signature. Write what you knew of their injuries.”
A miner asks how his household will survive the winter if work stops. Shao looks at him without promising compensation that has not been awarded.
Shao: “I don't know. But failing to answer that doesn't make the kiln safe.”
Pei: “This evidence supports closure for inspection and release of withheld money. Further compensation still needs review. We cannot call it approved today.”
Pei invites Shao to testify. Shao stays seated and asks whether the sealed order has been found.
Shao: “I agreed to speak publicly if we had the original. A crowd waiting doesn't change that.”
Gu: “Record mine, then. I admit the false deaths. As for Mu's order, we can't claim to possess a document we haven't recovered.”
Pei agrees to investigate what can be established, without supplying a conclusion for the missing evidence.
Quietly, Duan tells you, “You promised to tell me first. They were already outside my door when I heard. Getting the facts right afterward doesn't keep that promise.”
Pei reads the agreement aloud while Gu notes corrections. The first is the heading: “Charitable Relief” is crossed out and replaced with “Release of Debts and Accident Settlement.”
You: “Separate what is already owed from what is being added.”
Pei: “The hundred and forty stones are debts. Six months' lodging and work suited to their injuries are additional terms.”
Shao: “Who decides what work suits me?”
Pei: “A physician examines each person, then the work is discussed. Holding a brush won't be treated as proof you can carry ore. Another worker's condition won't substitute for yours.”
Gu: “Their identities?”
Pei: “Corrected in a sealed register. My negligence and your false report are reported separately, not erased by the settlement.”
Shao rests his hand in his lap. “And if it's still like this after six months?”
Pei: “A final settlement bars further claims arising from this accident, including injuries that do not heal.”
Tang moves the brushes out of reach and asks that this clause be explained separately to every claimant.
Tang lays his sister's letter beside the tickets. Two rooms are available without rent, but bedding must be brought. She offers shelter, not jobs for six people.
Shao: “If we cross, will they treat the debts as abandoned?”
Pei: “The departure papers will preserve your claims. If you wish to leave the sect, that can be recorded without waiving accident compensation.”
You: “Each of the other five gets their own papers?”
Pei: “Each signs and receives their own. Someone who stays won't be carried away by another's choice.”
Gu offers to go too. Shao asks him to stay and correct the false reports. After discussing it, Gu agrees to remain for the investigation.
Tang: “Retrieving the order cost half a day and the free tool space. People and bedding can travel as planned. The tools either stay in the village or cost eight stones to send separately.”
Tang: “The tools made the freight space and are loaded. At least they'll arrive with equipment they know how to use.”
Tang checks the harness and repeats that work must still be found across the river, and moving won't heal their injuries. Each of the six decides after hearing that.
Duan joins them after being sent for. Each of the seven claimants receives an agreement. Tang reads for those who need help, and Pei waits for questions before continuing to the next clause.
Duan: “These twenty stones are death relief, not payment for my silence.”
Pei: “They're already owed. Paying them now and waiving future claims are separate provisions.”
Shao: “The lodging lasts six months. What about the work?”
Pei: “The housing subsidy ends. Work continues under the individual employment terms. There is no lifetime guarantee.”
Shao: “Keep that sentence. Better an unpleasant answer than a misunderstanding.”
All seven eventually consent separately. Pei guarantees the lodging payments with his saved salary and cancels his next seclusion to carry out the arrangements.
Tang clarifies your role: a witness, neither a claimant collecting their money nor a guarantor of Pei's debt. If you oppose the waiver, your objection can be sealed and Tang can witness instead.
At the ferry, Shao hands over his own papers. When the boatman reads his name, he answers without explaining why the register once called him dead.
Duan hands the lining to one of his companions. “Find somewhere properly lit to sew it when you arrive. Don't strain your eyes.”
Shao: “You aren't coming?”
Duan: “People are collecting clothes tomorrow. I'll stay and keep the shop open.”
Shao: “We'll write once we're settled.”
Duan: “Sign your own name. Let me learn your handwriting.”
The other five board with whatever help their injuries require. Tang leaves the funeral cart with a neighbor and plans to collect it after everyone is settled.

The certified claim packet needs a keeper. Everyone has their departure papers, and the other party can retain copies. Whoever keeps the certified originals must produce them for future claims. Evidence never recovered remains missing.

Once temporary accommodation is arranged, Tang uses the tailor's table to record what happened. The six can receive visitors and will not return to the mine, but cannot leave freely before their identities are verified.
Duan: “Have their wages been paid?”
Tang: “Still withheld. There's no ruling and no signed settlement.”
Duan: “Then say that. Don't make accommodation sound like they've received everything.”
He lists the evidence recovered, then starts a separate column for what is missing. Kept or broken promises and any fighting are recorded as they happened.
Duan: “The two stones were payment for investigating. If already paid, they won't be paid again. If you declined them, they won't come back under another name.”
Tang: “Your account can be signed and submitted, or given privately to Duan. We can't withdraw testimony others have independently provided.”

After the closure notice is posted, each survivor receives twenty stones in wages, and Duan receives twenty in relief. Additional compensation remains under review. Gu's false reports and Pei's assignments enter the case separately.
Duan: “This time they haven't called it an accident nobody could prevent.”
Shao: “Have they apologized?”
Duan: “They've corrected the record. I'm keeping the old papers too. A correction shouldn't make their first account disappear.”
One neighbor stops buying cloth from her. His household depends on the mine and worries about winter. Duan understands, but will not tell the injured workers to return before inspection.
Shao: “I can testify. I can't promise everyone will be better off.”
Duan: “Then promise what you can actually do.”
Your testimony becomes part of the case. Some would ask for your help again; others wish you had never arrived. Reopening the mine and settling injury claims will still require attention.

The hundred and forty stones are divided among the seven claimants. Lodging is paid separately, and work assigned after individual medical assessments. The accounts finally distinguish old debts from new promises.
Shao: “I stopped after thirty lines today when my hand began hurting.”
Duan: “Did anyone make you continue?”
Shao: “No. I sat there a while anyway, expecting to be shouted at.”

Pei brings proof of the housing payment and reports that the ventilation controls have been replaced. Asked about Mu, he admits the supervisor remains in office, though he can no longer assign these six workers.
Duan: “Keep telling me about that when you come. Don't write only that everyone has settled.”

The injured have income and temporary housing, and have signed away further claims. Nobody knows what those claims might have brought. The agreement does not remove that uncertainty; it gives the coming months something firmer to rest on.

A letter from across the river arrives as Duan closes the shop. She dries her hands before opening it on the cutting table. Tang writes that all six have settled into the two cramped rooms and save fuel by cooking together.

Tang, in the letter: “We take suitable work when it comes, though not every day. Ning is learning to mend account tags with his left hand. He's slow, but nobody orders him to carry ore. I'll collect the cart once things settle here.”
A different, uneven hand adds a passage at the end.
Shao, in the letter: “When the door jammed, Jian said something very foul. I didn't dare mention it before. You asked us not to make him fearless, and I thought you might want to know.”
Duan smiles briefly, then looks down and folds the letter again.
Duan: “He said the same thing fixing our door.”

They left with their names, departure papers and preserved claims, not the hundred and forty stones still held upstream. Gu remains to correct the false reports. The agreed keeper retains the certified packet for the next opportunity to pursue the case.

The identity file moves between offices while the six remain in supervised accommodation. They have food and beds. Freedom to leave, unpaid wages and responsibility for the accident remain unresolved.
Duan: “Have they corrected Jian's page?”
Tang: “Yes. It records his burial. The other six are listed separately instead of being folded into seven bodies.”
Duan: “I was afraid they'd call him alive when they needed a signature and dead when they owed money.”

Tang preserves the evidence actually obtained and provides copies to those requesting them. Submitted statements remain on file; private reports are identified as private. Nobody invents testimony for a person who did not give it.

Duan returns the coat receipt to her book. Now she knows who wore the clothes, and knows her husband has not returned. The money she must keep asking about remains recorded. Replacing a page has erased none of it.
life.full_rewrite.life_event_missing_dis: Lin Que covered your last medicine delivery, and this round is yours.
