You come at the agreed time and find a notice accusing him of fleeing with a regulating ring. His cloak still hangs inside, with a dried medicine bowl beside the bed. It does not look like a room packed for departure.

A paper corner protrudes beneath the bed: “They aren't repairing the array. They're feeding it.” As you reach, a worker collecting the tray asks you to hold the edges so your thumb does not smear the damp writing.
You: “Do you know when he left?”
Worker: “I didn't see him leave. Nobody asked us before posting the notice.”
His forearm is bandaged, leaving one hand for the bowls. You steady the tray and ask who ordered Lin's belongings removed.
Worker: “Steward Xie. The bedding is to be gone before dark.”
You: “What's he trying to hide?”
Worker: “I know only that he gave the order. Ask him why. Don't write your suspicion as my testimony. I can't answer for that.”
The note does not locate Lin, but it deserves verification. You can begin with his room, the medicine accounts or Xie, or pass the request to someone who can take over.
The bowl smells bitter, similar to the wash on the worker's bandage. Rather than identifying medicine by smell alone, you ask who delivered it and what Lin was told.
Worker: “I carried the tray. He asked what it treated. I said aches, because that was what I was told.”
You: “Did you see him drink?”
Worker: “I didn't stay. I can't testify to that.”
Inside the cloak is a meal ticket for two. The next handover time is written on its back, matching the arrangement for you to take over.
Worker: “He often offered a meal after night duty. However late it got, he worried about people going home hungry.”
You: “Did he ask you to give me the note?”
Worker: “No. I found it collecting the bowl. He probably didn't know who would come first. Hiding it gave it some chance of surviving the clearance.”
You may carry Lin's cloak and ticket for safekeeping, not as your property. Leaving them where they are still allows you to trace the medicine through the accounts.
In the accounts room, a clerk bundles receipt copies beside a waiting brazier. The main medicine ledger is open, apparently listing the same batch under both infirmary and garden expenses.
You: “Are these being burned now?”
Clerk: “Xie ordered the copies destroyed. I received no other instruction.”

You point out the repeated batch number. The clerk says he did not make the entries. A delivery stub is stuck beneath the page, but he will not draw conclusions about the whole ledger from one glance.
Worker: “That medicine didn't reach our infirmary. I carried it below the garden.”
You: “Will you confirm that destination?”
Worker: “Yes. I know where I carried it. I don't know why the accounts say this.”
The clerk holds the ledger down and says it cannot leave without permission. If you take it anyway, responsibility must be yours rather than assigned to him.
You can examine approvals, batch numbers and destinations, preserve the entire ledger without authorization, or follow the worker's firsthand lead without taking it.
The available records do not reliably connect approvals, batch numbers and destinations. The worker points out that this neither disproves his account nor establishes that every entry is fraudulent.
Two verified approval stubs carry the same batch number but different destinations. The clerk confirms where the papers came from, not events he did not witness.
Xie is checking a garden temperature marker. At Lin's name, he sets it down and asks whether you read the notice.
You: “I read it. You say he took a regulating ring. Where is he?”
Xie: “He interfered with emergency medicine cultivation. Eight doses, with no replacements at the infirmary tonight.”
You: “That doesn't answer whether he is free to leave.”
Xie does not answer immediately. You explain finding the note and notice and request an inspection, rather than letting “desertion” end the inquiry.
Xie: “The space below cannot fill with spectators. I'll issue an inspection pass for the control room. Don't touch the live array before it's explained.”
You: “Put the access scope in writing and sign it.”
He brings paper and allows you to check it. You may instead hear the workers first or immediately request independent inspection by the duty elder.
The worker leads you through the kitchen passage. His duty key opens only the observation corridor; the control room has another lock. While using the key, he explains his injured arm.
Worker: “I tried lifting Lin and touched a hot fitting. I didn't break an array. I have no spirit root and don't know how.”
You: “Why was Lin there?”
Worker: “Five other disciples were there before. He freed them and couldn't leave himself. Ask him exactly where it went wrong.”
He presses the bandage edge down and keeps the wound away from the door. You support the tray so he can lay the key on a clean cloth.
You: “Will you give a written account?”
Worker: “Privately, yes. I still earn my wages here. Don't call out my name in the courtyard without asking.”
You: “Then I need to be clear about whether I accept that condition.”
Worker: “Yes. If you don't, I'll only guide you. Return the key afterward. The next shift needs the door.”

Through the observation rail, you see Lin seated within three connected seals. The regulating ring has not been carried away; it is locked into a fitting beside his wrist. Five other seats stand empty. He waits through a tremor before lifting his hand.
Lin: “Your medicine turn finally brought you here.”
You: “First I saw the desertion notice. How did freeing the others leave you trapped?”
Lin: “I thought it would stop. The return flow locked instead. Anyone here can see the ring. Apparently the notice can't.”
You: “Did you know how the supply would use people?”
Lin: “No. Two signed up because I told them night duty came with another meal. I wish I could take that back.”
You: “An extra meal isn't consent to be connected to an array.”
Lin: “I know. But they listened to me. I still owe them an explanation.”
You ask about stopping the garden to free him. He asks you to say that where Xie can hear, then requests no more unnamed medicine merely described as treating aches.
Lin: “Find out how to disconnect it. Don't simply pull the ring. Even afterward, I'll probably need help walking.”

The storeroom beside the corridor is outside the live array. Maintenance diagrams and night-duty sheets hang on the wall. A sealed box holds twenty-four charged stones. The worker points first to Xie's signed operating notes.
You: “Reduce supply, isolate the living-root connection, then drain the return flow?”
Worker: “Yes. I can read it. That doesn't make me qualified to declare the procedure safe.”
You: “Could the reserve replace Lin?”
Worker: “The ledger allows at most four hours. Enough for the remaining crop, not for all the earlier night shifts.”
You: “Not a substitute for the entire process, but one available now.”
Worker: “Xie approved leaving it unused. Check the date. It didn't just arrive.”

The signed sheets specify nights when living people supplied the array. Preserving them would secure technical evidence. Taking project stones is a separate act, and the worker does not hold the box key.
Worker: “If you go to the elder, say where these are. Don't claim we've replaced him already.”
A guard stops you outside the control-room floor marking. Lin remains visible behind the stone wall. He is not used as a hostage, but the supply does not stop while people argue at the door.
Guard: “Show an inspection pass if you have one. Otherwise wait for Xie to open it.”
You: “Every delay keeps draining him.”
Guard: “I've sent for Xie. Authorized inspection is one thing; allowing someone to strike a live array is another.”
Worker: “We asked yesterday too. Nobody freed him.”
The guard looks inside but holds his position. He urges the messenger again. Xie's returning footsteps can now be heard on the upper stair.
You can enter with an existing pass or wait for Xie's explanation. Forcing the doorway would create a fight with the guard, not replace the shutdown procedure.
The worker moves behind the wall to stay with Lin, clearing the doorway and stating that he will not join a fight.
You enter the cleared antechamber and the guard raises a hand to stop you. The worker stays with Lin behind the wall. The upper passage remains open for withdrawal to the elder.
Guard: “Whoever falls here, the supply inside won't stop by itself.”
You: “Then let me in to deal with it.”
Guard: “You need authority and a qualified operator. Stand down. The steward is on his way.”
Hearing them, Lin braces against the seat and shifts his feet.
Lin: “You're arguing about who gets through a door. I'm waiting for someone to undo the connection. If you fight, remember that still has to happen afterward.”
The worker will not cross a battlefield to fetch tools or connect his injured arm to the array. You must rely on combat abilities you already have and can presently use.
The guard has not struck. Withdrawing now for formal intervention will not be recorded as a fight.

Once access is secured, Xie opens the service cover, checks the ring beside Lin's wrist and lays out the external isolation tools. Pulling the ring would trigger return flow; disconnection must follow the proper sequence.
You: “You know the procedure. Can you free him now?”
Xie: “Yes. Shutting down the garden would lose this crop.”
Lin: “You said eight emergency doses. Do you know eight people will die tonight, or is that the most frightening way to keep me seated?”
Xie: “They would need substitutes. I don't know how long obtaining them would take.”
You ask about another power source. Xie explains that twenty-four reserve stones can cover the remaining hours, though not the full growing cycle.
Lin: “Then replacement has been possible for this stage. You kept refusing to spend the reserve.”
Xie admits that he approved saving the stones. He does not blame the worker who cannot cast.
You: “Whichever route is chosen, nobody else takes his place.”

Xie: “Agreed. I can shut it down, or replace him with the reserve, free him, harvest and remove the living-source fittings. You can check the external tools without manipulating spiritual energy yourself.”
Xie repeats the complete sequence while the worker checks the external markers. You can supervise whether the procedure is followed without claiming that this makes you an array operator.
Xie: “Reduce supply and isolate the living connection. Wait for the return flow to drain. Nobody opens the seat early.”
Lin: “The numbness is easing, but it's shaking. I know not to move. Keep going.”
Only after the last return flow drains does Xie open the fittings. Lin leans on the rail without forcing himself upright. The worker calls for medical staff and a chair.
Lin: “This time, tell me what's in the medicine.”
Worker: “The healer will explain. I won't vouch for something I don't understand again.”
The growing beds lose their heat. The crop will not mature on schedule. Its loss must be recorded, while the freed person still requires treatment. Disconnection is not recovery.
The worker puts Lin's entrusted cloak around him and returns the ticket. Lin feels its corner and puts it away without promising to use it tonight.
The infirmary provides an ordinary blanket and records his actual injuries and care needs.
Xie opens the reserve box before everyone and counts the twenty-four charged stones. They belong to the project. Their use is entered in the incident account, not added to your belongings.
Xie: “After replacement, the desertion notice comes down and sick leave is recorded. Once the crop is harvested, every living-source connection is removed.”
Lin: “Will you publicly explain why the notice was false?”
Xie: “Under this arrangement, that explanation is sealed for the elder.”
Lin: “I understand what you're trying to keep private. Treatment must not require waiving complaints, and we each get our own records.”
Xie agrees and relinquishes control over Lin's future duty assignments. Individual records go to their subjects, without granting anyone access to other patients' private information.
Watching Xie's hands, Lin asks to be ready before the procedure begins. A chair waits outside. He will be freed immediately after replacement, not kept seated until the harvest.
You: “The other option remains. Refuse now and the array is shut down, without using another person as reserve.”

Lin is brought to the courtyard in a chair and does not force himself to stand for the hearing. The elder clears unnecessary onlookers and asks which evidence identifies repeated authorization of living power sources.
Elder: “The complete medicine ledger can establish approvals. Duty sheets alone need confirmation from someone who knows how they were used.”
Xie objects to posting patients' names. Lin agrees that unrelated medical details and identities should be redacted, while the approving official's marks remain visible.
Lin: “My name may remain. Nobody worried about privacy when accusing me of desertion.”
Worker: “I'll confirm my part privately. Don't read it to the courtyard.”
Elder: “Identity sealed, events public. The clerk will follow that scope.”
Lin asks for his chair to be turned toward the worker and waits until he understands and agrees before continuing. Being helped does not give Lin authority to decide for him.
The ruling can extend only as far as the evidence. You may instead seek protection first or lodge the material and withdraw from directing the case.
You request an inquiry from the duty elder. He has the clerk distinguish firsthand observations, others' accounts and unverified suspicions rather than treating the note as a verdict.
Elder: “Begin with what you know. If you haven't located him, say he needs locating. Don't add a scene to make me take this seriously.”
When Xie returns to the regulating ring, the elder asks whether Lin can leave. An object's location cannot substitute for a person's condition.
Xie: “An inspection doesn't need this crowd.”
Elder: “Then I'll send medical staff. If he remains connected, end the living supply under supervision.”
You: “Without waiting for the entire audit?”
Elder: “Punishment requires evidence. A dangerous practice that can be stopped now need not wait for an audit.”

Xie mentions the crop loss. The elder orders it recorded and replacements arranged. You must decide whether to honor the witness's confidentiality. Needing testimony does not automatically authorize publishing a name.
Hearing his name spread through the courtyard, the worker tells you quietly, “I was clear. I asked, and you agreed.” He keeps his papers instead of handing them to you.

The infirmary confirms that Lin is disconnected and receiving treatment. If shutdown was still needed, Xie has completed it under independent supervision. A person already freed is not reconnected merely to repeat a procedure.
Elder: “Living supply on night duty is suspended. The surviving accounts remain under investigation. Lin's present status can be restored before every other responsibility is decided.”
Lin: “Write down whom I contact next. Don't send me back to Xie with the same paper.”
Elder: “A separate officer receives testimony. Xie may not operate living-source arrays during review. His other duties remain for now.”
The worker asks when substitute medicine will arrive. The elder admits it cannot be ready tonight. Contacting suppliers is not described as delivery.
Unauthorized removal of records, fighting or disclosure is reviewed separately. Pending censure and archive restrictions can be contested, but freeing Lin does not automatically erase them.
The protection order can take effect while disputed points are appealed. It establishes immediate safeguards, not proof of every suspicion.

The worker brings the duty key and surviving papers to the infirmary and asks that the urgent matter be registered first. With his uninjured hand on the desk, he distinguishes his knowledge from what others told him.
Clerk: “I need the duty officer. What was the situation when you left?”
Worker: “Lin is still connected. This is a request for rescue, not paperwork after one.”
Worker: “He's disconnected. Treatment and accountability need continuing. Don't record him as still bound there.”
Worker: “Someone must verify the situation below. The note and notice conflict. We can't decide from this desk that he fled.”
The clerk places the papers where they can be seen and calls medical staff. The worker asks to wait seated instead of holding a door with his injured arm.
Clerk: “Did the person who first came looking promise to continue?”
Worker: “Record what was actually said. Sign only with authorization. Don't invent it for convenience.”

When the new duty list is posted, Lin first asks for the correction beside it to be read aloud: the desertion accusation is withdrawn. Private medical details are redacted. Xie loses control of night assignments, and another officer handles the investigation.
Lin: “No new assignment beside my name this time?”
Worker: “Not until the healer establishes what you can do.”
Lin: “Keep me a copy. I don't want it turned into my refusal to work in two days.”

The worker says substitute medicine has been ordered without a confirmed arrival. Lin does not celebrate. He asks that medical staff answer patients' questions instead of leaving tray carriers to guarantee officials' claims.
You: “When you can sit through a meal comfortably, we'll have one together.”
Lin: “Bring him too and let him choose somewhere. Not the duty kitchen again.”
The name is corrected. Injuries, unpaid work and responsibility still require follow-through. A promise to meet later does not become a cultivation technique or an extra share of compensation.

Xie connects the twenty-four reserve stones through the witnessed procedure. Once the living connection is isolated, Lin is immediately helped outside to rest. Hours later the crop is harvested, the array shut down and the living-source fittings removed.
The worker shows Lin the new notice. It says sick leave, without explaining the earlier desertion accusation.
Lin: “Agreeing to a sealed account doesn't make those words feel right.”
Xie: “The medicine has gone to the infirmary.”
Lin: “It should. Don't use that to ask for my congratulations.”
He rechecks his complaint rights, record copies and reassignment to another steward. Treatment does not waive his claims, and accepting medicine does not mean he volunteered to power the array.
The worker keeps his own copy without receiving access to everyone else's medical details.

Eight doses are preserved and living supply has ended. Responsibility remains in a sealed file, while the public notice offers a convenient sick-leave explanation. Lin rests in his chair, accepting the result that freed him today without surrendering the right to question it later.

A temporary protection order replaces the desertion notice. Lin's present status is restored, living-source duty ends for him, and the infirmary continues care. The whole case is not declared resolved.
Lin: “I still dislike 'temporary.' It sounds as if it could disappear again.”
Worker: “The responsible officer and review process are written down. At least we know where to ask.”
Lin asks whether the worker will return to his old shift. He will; he needs the wages. Lin starts to advise him, stops, and instead asks him to keep records of any change.
Lin: “Continuing to work doesn't mean forgiveness. I shouldn't put those words in your mouth.”
Lost crops, injured people and the false notice still need investigation. Actual misconduct can be contested separately; careful reporting alone does not invent an offense.
The worker keeps his own documents afterward. Lin's safety does not make the disclosed name private again or restore the trust you broke.

After the infirmary receives the papers, the worker insists that “report received” and “matter resolved” remain separate entries. The key lies beside them so the next officer can inspect the site rather than wait for another appeal.
Clerk: “Confirm once more: had he been disconnected when you left?”

The worker checks the actual state again. A freed person requires continuing treatment and inquiry. Someone still connected remains an urgent rescue request. What nobody personally saw is marked for verification.
Worker: “Don't stamp it completed to reassure me. I'd rather know what remains.”
The clerk returns a copy and sends medical staff out with the key. The worker can finally sit and tend his own injury instead of carrying every message alone.

The original participant's signatures and promises are retained only as actually authorized. Unconsciousness or death produces no invented later conversation, and an unfinished rescue earns no completion reward.

The infirmary receives the surviving material and preserves Lin's actual rescue state and evidence. The worker can no longer add testimony. Those taking over must verify what remains, without signing for him or declaring an unfinished rescue successful.
The ferry is tied up when you reach Rain Ferry, but Old He does not invite you aboard. He brightens the lamp beneath the eaves and asks you to listen. Beside the old landing, rain runs down a rusted sword embedded in mud. A voice keeps asking whether the last boat has returned.
He: “It belonged to Duan Qing, one of the soldiers. He died here forty-three years ago. I was a boy rowing the ferry then.”
You: “Is that his spirit speaking?”
He: “A remnant. It hears us, but seems to think that night has never ended.”
The question comes again. He raises a hand before you answer. He once said the boat had returned, he explains, only to be asked who was aboard. At the answer “nobody,” water surged into the shed.
You: “That's why you've closed the crossing.”
He: “I won't take passengers when it starts asking. But keeping the crossing shut doesn't tell me when it will end.”
He entrusts you with a wooden ferry token. Names are cut around a military seal, with arrival marks on the back. Black wax obscures the lowest line.
He: “I was the one who promised to return for him. If you're willing to investigate, hear the whole account. If not, don't make a promise merely to quiet it.”
In the shed, He sets out water and cloth, placing a narrow knife out of reach so it will not be used casually on the token. He points to three clear names and says all three reached the far bank.
You: “Did you cut all these marks?”
He: “Yes, after arrival. I won't say I did everything right. Those three marks are true.”
You: “Why is the lower line covered in wax?”
He: “Wax from the lamp. I never cleared it. Whenever I wiped down that far, I stopped.”

You angle it toward the lamp and make out only a few crowded strokes. He says the wax can be soaked loose or the lettering examined in the available light, but guessed words must not be carved into it.
You: “What does waiting cost us?”
He: “Tonight's calm water. Miss it and we wait until tomorrow. Travelers need somewhere else to sleep, and I keep the ferry closed.”
He places the water before you and explains how to support the token without loosening its existing cuts.

He first explains that Duan had orders to guard the grain stores but left to protect civilians. As you approach the sword, an outline gathers along its spine, one arm incomplete and its gaze fixed on an abandoned mooring post.
Duan's remnant: “Has the ferryman returned? We still need a line on this side.”
You: “There's no line here now. I've come to ask about that night.”
Duan's remnant: “No line? I can still feel it pulling.”
It looks down at the missing arm, disperses slightly, and gathers again.
You: “Why did you leave the grain stores?”
Duan's remnant: “They were closing the gates. A girl was trying to lift her mother over a wall and couldn't reach. If I'd stayed by the grain sacks, they wouldn't have got through.”
You: “You knew you were disobeying?”
Duan's remnant: “Yes. But the questioning has to wait until everyone has crossed. Did they get aboard?”
You say you have not verified that yet. It asks you to check rather than offer comforting assurances. Behind you, He remains silent.
The lettering beneath the wax becomes readable: “Return for the defender.” Space for an arrival mark remains empty. He looks at it without pretending he does not know whom it means.
He brings an old household register from the cupboard. The three passengers appear in it, with later dates of moving, marrying and eventually dying.
He: “The woman ran a food stall afterward, the farmer planted fields again, and the child grew up. I saw more of their lives than one landing.”
You: “Then the shadows aren't those three souls trapped here.”
He: “They're impressions left in the sword. It still worries about people who went on to live long lives.”
A receipt slips out as he turns a page. It instructs the boat to return for the defender. He steadies its corner without putting it away.
You: “You kept this for forty-three years too.”
He: “I thought of throwing it away, then kept putting it back. With only the passenger marks, it would look as if everything had been completed.”
He offers to copy the names and arrivals onto paper from the fare book and read it aloud to you. The originals remain at the ferry for others to examine.
The lettering beneath the wax cannot be read reliably. He puts away the knife, preferring delay to treating a guess as the token's answer.
Shallows separate the old landing from the river. After sounding the depth, He points to the ferry's keel and explains that it draws too much water.
You: “We'd need a shallow boat?”
He: “Or dismantle my deck for a raft. I own the boat, but my regular passengers would have to take the ridge path afterward.”
You: “You didn't mention that cost before.”
He: “I hoped you might have a suitable boat and spare me saying it. Now you know. Decide with that included.”
Back in the shed, he takes an old rope from a dry cupboard. Its clean end was not torn apart by the current.
He: “And the sword has been holding the dangerous current down. Once the oath ends, night crossings can't continue as before, whether the sword is taken away or not.”
You: “The passengers need to be told.”
He: “I'll tell them. We can inspect the route first. Preparing it doesn't commit us to dismantling anything.”
He brings the rope and register to the bank, confirming that the three passengers reached safety. Then he lays the cut end upward across his knees and tells you about the promised return.
He: “Duan released the short mooring line but kept the long rope in his hand. I promised to return for him after landing.”
You: “How were the three passengers?”
He: “The woman couldn't breathe. The farmer had an injured arm. The girl bailed with both shoes and kept asking whether her mother was dying.”
You: “You were afraid the boat wouldn't make it back?”
He: “I was afraid none of us would make it across. I cut the rope and rowed for the far bank.”
You: “Did Duan see?”
He looks at the cut and nods. “He saw the knife. I kept saying I'd saved the passengers. I wouldn't say he watched me abandon him.”

At dawn He returned in an empty boat and found Duan dead beside the sword. Saving three people and breaking his promise happened on the same night. The household register had preserved only half that account.
He: “Record it however it needs to be recorded. Don't turn my knife into a rope broken by water.”
The waiting passengers gather beneath the eaves. He tells them about cutting the rope. At the detail of the girl bailing with her shoes, a woman carrying a covered lamp says the girl was her mother.
Woman: “She told me about that night. Everyone was terrified. Don't improve the story by pretending you knew you'd save them.”
He: “I didn't know. I was afraid to row back.”
You explain that the ferry may be dismantled and the river's old protection will end with the oath. People ask how to send grain and calculate extra help for carrying it over the ridge.
He: “I know what trouble this causes you.”
Woman: “Then don't settle for saying everyone understands. My grain still needs delivering. If I complain in two days, hear that too.”
He agrees to post the hours and reasons for closure. She leaves her lamp on the bench and offers to hear the rest, without announcing forgiveness on everyone else's behalf.
Woman: “Keep the names somewhere dry. Even if this isn't settled tonight, don't give the next visitor only half the story.”

Late at night, three images appear beside the old landing: a woman with an empty bundle, a farmer trailing a broken rope, and a child. He reads their names and arrival dates from the register. The images do not answer, but the voice in the sword listens.
Duan's remnant: “What happened to the girl?”
He: “She grew up and had a child. Her daughter still lives here and came for the ferry today.”
Duan's remnant: “Then who is the last one? I've been waiting for him to board.”
You: “The boat was meant to return for the defender. You were the person left behind.”
He tells the rope-cutting account again, facing the sword. This time the passengers' rescue does not replace the account of his failure to return.
Duan's remnant: “I was still looking for the boy. I didn't understand that you'd grown old.”
He: “I'm here. But Duan himself never lived to see it.”
The three passenger images fade. Still bound to the sword, the remnant recognizes its own unfinished return. It will consent either to being carried across or to discussing release.
Duan's remnant: “If you simply take the sword by force, I'll resist. Possessing the weapon won't make the missing boat's return a fact.”
He places a reed mat by the steps for wrapping the blade, making clear that this is not consent to taking it. The remnant gathers its outline again in front of the sword.
You: “Leaving it here means more waiting.”
Duan's remnant: “You've heard two paths I am willing to take. Your impatience doesn't leave force as the only one.”
You: “Can you leave the sword?”
Duan's remnant: “No, and I cannot move it. Someone must carry it for me to cross. Otherwise I remain on this bank.”
He withdraws to the steps and says he will not fight. The remnant agrees not to attack the ferryman or pursue someone retreating onto the steps.
He: “What you do afterward is another matter. I'll record how you obtained it tonight.”
Duan's remnant: “You asked who would own the sword first. I understand now which matter concerns you most.”
The blade remains in the mud. No blow has been struck. You can return to negotiation, leave, or challenge it with abilities you actually possess.
He moves the lamp behind the steps to mark the retreat and leaves the fighting ground. The sword lifts slightly against its binding, muddy water dripping from the tip.
Duan's remnant: “Stand down now and we can keep speaking. Once we fight, changing your mind won't undo the damage.”
You: “You'll stop if I retreat to the steps?”
Duan's remnant: “I defend the sword. I won't pursue you. Keep the ferryman out of it as well.”
Beside the lamp, He answers, “The light stays here. You can see the way out. Don't cling to a sword until you can't leave.”
River water slicks the stones. You check your footing. The remnant's willingness to fight has changed neither your available techniques nor your existing injuries.
The remnant waits for your answer without striking at your hesitation.

The guard breaks, leaving a thin outline beside the sword. The remnant no longer recognizes the river clearly, but keeps asking which bank the boat should approach. He waits until you are clear of the blade before descending the steps.
You: “Could carrying the sword across now complete the promise?”
Duan's remnant: “Neither bank fits my memory now. You could carry me across without my recognizing the return.”
He: “The fight scattered it. We can't carry it across and record a completed arrival it cannot recognize.”
You: “Can the oath still be released?”
He: “The passengers' arrival is established, and it has heard its own account. We can still ask for its consent.”
There is no longer a guard strong enough to stop you taking it. Another fight is unnecessary. Leaving it will not reverse the damage already done.
He: “If you take it, I'll record a taking after combat. Not a gift from me, or a gift he agreed to make.”
He waits for safe, calm water and checks the shallow approach again. Cut lines mark the deck, but no boards have been removed. Any boat of yours must first pass his checks for draft and load.
He: “Using my boards means rebuilding the ferry. A suitable shallow boat avoids that, but it must actually be here. We can't wish one into existence.”
You: “Does the remnant prefer either?”
Duan's remnant: “Either that reaches the bank. I am waiting for the return, not the original planks.”
He checks the entrusted token and prepares a support to secure the blade. An experienced boatman will handle the crossing; nobody needs to board holding an exposed edge.
You: “After landing, you and I still need to return safely.”
He: “Of course. We're carrying a remnant across, not leaving another living person behind.”
Duan's remnant: “Call my name. Then I'll know we've landed.”
After checking the preparations, He waits. He may choose to dismantle his own ferry, but nobody else's property can be appropriated to settle his old debt.
You return the token to He. Laying it on dry stone beside the sword, he proposes acknowledging the past and ending the wait without reenacting the crossing.
Duan's remnant: “You won't promise to return again?”
He: “I'm here already. Another promise cannot bring back the man I failed to collect.”
You ask whether the remnant will release the demand. It studies He for a long time, finally recognizing the elderly man as the boy it remembers.
Duan's remnant: “Keep the passengers' names, and keep the fact that I was left on the bank.”
He: “Both. Your silence won't let me omit that part again.”
You remind He that release will end the protection for night crossings. He says he will operate according to ordinary daylight conditions and stop collecting night fares.
Duan's remnant: “Then do what we've agreed. Don't destroy proof of anyone else's arrival to make me disappear.”
You mention your own promise to complete the crossing and ask to replace it with agreed release. The remnant explicitly consents. He records the change without calling it a physical crossing.
He reads each name and arrival mark and asks how the record should be kept. The token may remain at the ferry, or a complete copy may be preserved before returning the wood to the river.
You: “The original cannot go without a copy.”
He: “Then I'll copy it now and read it back. There's no reason to save a few sheets at the expense of the record.”
Duan's remnant: “The seal was originally for grain accounts. When we used it for people, I was afraid of missing a name.”
He: “Yours needs adding after the three, marked as not collected.”
Duan's remnant: “Write that.”
He pauses with the brush, then finishes the sentence. Both paper and token lie under the lamp. Nobody urges him to skip the line he finds hardest to read.
He lowers the barrier and posts the night closure beside the fares. Waiting passengers ask how much longer they must wait. This time he does not promise service tomorrow night.
He: “The oath isn't released. Use the ridge path. Daylight service depends on the water.”
Villager: “You owe us an explanation of why.”

He writes down the rope-cutting, the passengers' arrival and Duan's death before the return. His own memories are identified as his own, and assistance from others is recorded only as far as it actually went.
He: “Anyone able to give an account can write it or dictate it. If someone cannot answer, I won't invent their agreement.”
Villager: “You could have told us the first part years ago.”
He: “Yes. Give this to the next person willing to investigate. They shouldn't have to begin with guesses.”
The entrusted token must still be returned. Existing promises and injuries do not disappear because the investigation stops here.
On landing, He secures the boat before calling Duan's name. A ripple spreads across the water. The outline beside the sword looks down as though recognizing a place finally kept for its arrival.
Duan's remnant: “Nobody left behind?”
He: “Nobody. We've checked this time.”

The remnant fades. Rust falls from the blade, which He wraps before handing it to you with a warning against testing the edge by hand. He still has work at the ferry and does not keep the sword for himself.
Back home, the dismantled ferry remains on the bank. Grain must go over the ridge while He finds the timber and labor to rebuild.
He: “Warning you about dismantling it doesn't make carrying grain easier. I'll give you a repair date when I actually have one.”
He returns your inspected boat in its actual condition, without producing a second one or pretending earlier damage has vanished.
He: “Night crossings still stop. The sword no longer restrains the current. Having a boat doesn't mean the river is unchanged.”

He takes back the token and adds the final arrival mark, specifying that the passenger was Duan's remnant. The broken promise of forty-three years ago remains recorded. This crossing finally has its own date.
At release, the blade breaks into pale light and disperses into the rain, leaving no weapon to collect. He sits on the steps and listens until he is sure the question has not returned.
He: “I thought I would need to hear forgiveness before knowing it was over.”
You: “He agreed to end the wait. He didn't change that night for you.”
He: “I'll remember that.”
He stores the preserved names and arrival records in the fare chest, checking Duan's entry carefully.
A woman arrives with grain for the night boat and is unhappy to hear it is closed. He does not tell her to celebrate the released oath. He helps move her sack somewhere dry.
Woman: “My brother is still waiting for this.”
He: “We'll check the water at dawn. If we still can't cross, I'll ask about porters for the ridge.”
You leave without the sword. The ferry has lost the repeated question and the protection for night travel. Those still living must work out the consequences for themselves.
When the sword leaves the mud, the bank quickly falls quiet. He pushes the reed mat toward you to cover the blade, then takes back the entrusted token and puts it in his cupboard.
You: “You'll still help wrap it?”
He: “Preventing a cut doesn't mean approving how you took it.”
Even wrapped, the sword speaks. The remnant cannot distinguish the bank it seeks and does not accept its defeated guard as a completed crossing.
Duan's remnant: “Which bank are we approaching? Don't leave anyone here again.”
You: “I thought winning would quiet it.”
He: “It can't stop you now. That isn't the same as forgetting what it's waiting for.”

He records that the sword was taken after combat and the oath remains unresolved, then lowers the night barrier. You possess the actual blade and carry its unfinished waiting. Any future resolution must begin with what happened today.

The next visitor first sees the closure notice, then the account beneath the lamp. He sits beside it, reading for those who need help. He no longer waits to be questioned before admitting he cut the rope.
Visitor: “You're the ferryman in this account?”
He: “Yes. Three people crossed. Duan did not live to see me return.”
Visitor: “The person who came to help didn't settle it either.”
He: “Their work and where it stopped are recorded next. Read it before treating an unfinished task as no help at all.”
Asked whether the visitor must take on the old promise, He says to hear the full account first and decide freely. A new visitor is no longer an excuse to erase everything that came before.
The oath remains, as does any weakness caused by combat. No sword is delivered. The written testimony may at least spare the next person some mistaken guesses.

Later visitors read He's account at the ferry, with no chance to question him in person. It distinguishes the three passengers' arrival, the defender's death and the unfulfilled promise, and records how far the later investigation proceeded.
The oath is unresolved, and no sword is handed to anyone. Existing testimony and injuries remain as they were. The record gives no new speech to someone no longer there.
life.full_rewrite.life_story_salt_basket: Salt purchased jointly by seventeen households has not arrived. Ruan Qiao, who organized the delivery, invites you into her shop and lays out three purchase tallies beside a route map. Rain is falling higher up, and the hauler Tian Rang has not even sent word that he is safe.
Ruan: “Three baskets, each holding a sealed sack worth six stones. Rang checked every seal when he collected them.”
You: “Was he hauling them alone?”
Ruan: “With the sect's spirit deer, which he normally tends. Man, deer and salt are all missing, and people are already calling it banditry.”
You: “You don't believe that?”
Ruan: “I haven't seen it, so I won't invent a story. Find out and give me the truth. I'll pay three stones.”
Separately, she entrusts you with six stones for recovering the freight. Record actual expenses and return the remainder.
Outside, a child rings a toy bell. Ruan asks him to put it away. Rang uses a similar sound to call the deer; if it returns frightened, children must not lure it into the crowd.
Ruan: “Expenses and your fee are separate. Tell me bad news too. I won't call your work worthless because I dislike the answer.”

A young handler crouches beside the broken mountain road with a cut strap at her feet. She introduces herself as Ye Sui, Rang's apprentice. When you ask about the salt, she checks your tallies before pointing down to a stone shelf.
Ye: “Two sacks are caught behind the pillar, seals intact. The third went into the stream. There's nothing useful left to recover.”
You: “Where are the signs of bandits?”
She crouches again and takes her hand away from the spilled salt.
Ye: “There aren't any. I repeated my master's story. I didn't see bandits or examine the tracks.”
You: “Will you take me to him now?”
Ye: “Yes. The deer is called Eleven. Its prints go uphill without signs of dragging. Hear why he cut the load before deciding what to call him.”

She explains that the old stairs reach the salt safely. Four stones will hire porters with frames, or someone physically able can spend the afternoon carrying it. Heavier rain may wash away the shelf.

Transport Steward Xu Ce is having a grain cart weighed again. Ye, Rang's apprentice, waits beside a broken buckle she brought back. Xu orders two excess sacks unloaded before turning to the missing deer.
Xu: “Authorization covered three baskets on sound tack. It appears that saddle should not have been used again.”
You: “If you know it's injured, why send a capture party?”
Xu: “A frightened spirit beast is loose above occupied homes. It needs supervision before it reaches them, not after someone is hurt.”
You: “Could you catch it yourself?”
Xu: “Catching up isn't the same as pursuing safely. If it jumps onto someone's roof, my realm won't replace their house.”

He shows the route deposit: Rang lodged eighteen stones. Verified freight loss is deducted, and the remainder stays his. The sect owns the deer, which cannot simply be handed over as payment for salt.
Xu: “I can suspend capture until tomorrow's hearing. The injuries and salt still need accounting for. Years of care don't exempt anyone.”
Outside the old watchtower, Ye soaks the saddle pad. Dried blood has worked into the weave. The broken buckle bends inward toward where it lay against Eleven's flank.
Ye: “He said a thicker pad would do. I saw the blood and still waited for him to tell me whether it mattered.”
You: “Were you afraid to contradict him?”
Ye: “And I wanted to believe he understood more. Last autumn he said Eleven's carrying days were over. Then he accepted winter work.”
A hoof scrapes inside the tower. Ye slows her movements. Eleven now watches every raised hand, she explains; even a water bowl must be shown before approaching.
You: “Will Rang speak with us?”
Ye: “He wants the dusk patrol to pass first. I know hiding won't settle it, but let him speak before someone sees a lead rope and takes the deer.”
You: “The bandit story needs correcting too.”
Ye: “I said it myself. I can sign my own correction instead of always hiding behind what my master told me.”
Porters from the ruined temple inspect the site with their own carrying frames. The two sacks' seals match Ruan's tallies. The shortcut is crumbling, while the old stairs remain sound.
Porter: “Four stones for both sacks by the long route. The third is gone. We won't pretend it's recoverable.”
You: “What if they stay here tonight?”
Porter: “Once water passes that pillar, the shelf is at risk. Decide now if you want them moved.”
Ye checks that the new frames have no inward-pointing buckles. Carrying the sacks yourselves would take the afternoon and miss the day's market.
You: “Recovering the salt doesn't replace your correction.”
Ye: “I know. It belongs to the households. It isn't something I can use to purchase forgiveness.”

With route and cargo checked, you can hire help, carry within your physical limits, or use a genuinely suitable learned movement technique. You can also go to Rang first, leaving the salt exposed to the night's rain.
At dusk, Rang finally comes out of the watchtower. Eleven is unsaddled, its flank abraded but all four legs bearing weight. Rang's bell is wrapped tightly in cloth and remains silent.
Rang: “Don't touch the bell. Even frightened, it will come when it hears that sound.”
You: “Did you cut away the salt?”
Rang: “The buckle caught it. When it lunged toward the edge, the load pulled outward. I cut the rope to keep it from dragging the deer down.”
You: “You'd seen the blood on the pad before that.”
Rang: “Yes. I thought it could manage one more trip, then I'd replace it.”
Ye: “Last year's final season became more trips for the same reason.”

Rang explains that his roof leaks and he still owes repairs to a beam Eleven cracked in Ruan's shed. That is why he accepted the salt job. Then he shakes his head and admits none of those debts was the deer's promise to pay.
Rang: “I raised it. I kept wanting that to prove I knew better than anyone how to care for it.”
You: “Now you can see that raising it and continuing to hurt it can both be true.”

He wraps the bell into his bag and agrees to face Ruan's loss account in the morning. Ye suggests inspecting the northern deer route too, rather than treating wild deer on the mountain as proof of a safe release.
At dawn, Ye takes you above the tower. Three cliff deer move through the pines. The old northern path skirts the fields, but its final stretch disappears behind a ridge.
Ye: “Eleven once lived with a herd. This is worth examining, but seeing deer isn't the same as checking the route.”
You: “They may not accept it even if we release it here.”
Ye: “Then we don't promise acceptance. First establish that it can walk the whole route unladen, without jumping a gap while injured.”
A loose tile falls from the tower. Eleven moves somewhere quieter. Rang allows slack in the lead rather than immediately pulling it back.
You: “Choosing a spot in the yard doesn't prove it can find food in the hills.”
Ye: “I know. Wanting the option means admitting what we don't know too.”

Completing the inspection requires passing Ruan's upper orchard gate and checking the path beyond. If the terrain exceeds your present abilities, you can stop and accurately report only what you have seen.

Ruan arrives with the morning travelers. The night rain has damaged the stone shelf. She first checks the salt actually recovered and the freight expenses, then shows Rang the households' contributions.
Ruan: “Those weren't three baskets of your own goods. I've heard why you cut the load. Hiding and leaving everyone waiting is another matter.”
Rang: “Deduct the loss from my deposit. I accept that.”
Ruan: “Six per lost sack. If two were recovered, twelve remain. If all were lost, nothing remains. My anger doesn't change the rate.”
Ye asks about Eleven. Ruan offers the fenced lower orchard through the spring market for twelve stones, including fodder. Anything afterward must be renegotiated.
Rang: “Would the sect agree?”
Ruan: “Xu must sign. There's also the retirement station, or a verified northern route. Those belong at the hearing, not in a decision made by me alone.”

She pays your three-stone investigation fee and takes back the remaining freight money separately. Establishing the facts completes your commission. Compensation and care still need their own arrangements.
Ruan: “Recovering two sacks helped, but we missed yesterday's market. I'll explain that too. Recovering cargo doesn't erase delay.”
Two search disciples arrive at the lower gate with a care-station takeover order. Eleven stops at the sight of the lead. Ye moves it behind the stone wall, leaving a wide passage clear.
Disciple: “Supervised care first, then the steward's hearing.”
Rang: “It hasn't hurt anyone here. Why take it now?”
Disciple: “Care cannot wait for an injury. Show a suspension order if you have one. Otherwise we follow this document.”
Ruan first asks them to keep ropes away from the wound. They agree and offer to record the destination and responsible carer.
Rang: “Last time it was care too. Then they saddled it again.”
You: “You saddled it too. This time the no-carrying condition needs writing, not another person saying to trust them.”
Neither disciple has drawn a weapon. You may show a valid order, accept registered care or prevent removal. Eleven will not be used as a combatant in the dispute.
You move into the empty cart yard. The disciples follow and draw their weapons. Ruan moves the onlookers back. Ye keeps Eleven behind the wall, and Rang leaves the wrapped bell in his bag.
Disciple: “Stand aside now and the care transfer will still be registered as agreed.”
You: “I want the hearing first.”
Disciple: “We need a valid order, not a new demand from someone in the yard.”
Ruan looks at you. “If you fight, keep the deer out of it. Whoever wins, the salt account remains.”
Ye checks that the gate behind you remains open and tells Rang not to block it. The younger disciple glances at the lead set aside and holds position near his companion.
The decision to fight is yours. It will not heal Eleven's flank or recover freight already lost.
In an enclosed yard, Xu examines Eleven's wound and unladen movement. He confirms it can bear weight without describing it as healed.
Xu: “Every arrangement will prohibit carrying riders or freight, including during review.”
Rang: “Who checks that afterward?”
Xu: “The receiving carer keeps daily records, with copies at the sect. Anyone discovering a saddle can raise a complaint under those terms.”
Ruan verifies the deposit settlement first. Actual losses are paid and the remainder returned to Rang, rather than treating all his money as available for others to allocate.
Xu: “Winter in the orchard needs funding. The station has an approved retirement place. Release requires a verified complete route and a current mobility assessment.”
Ye: “And if no arrangement is agreed?”
Xu: “Supervised accommodation while review continues, not an automatic return to work.”
Rang reminds you, “You promised no removal before the hearing. The takeover came first. It's good we're talking now, but record that promise honestly too.”
Ruan shows you the lower orchard. The fence is sound, but the shelter needs a new latch. Rang measures it and asks what the twelve stones cover before talking about earning money repairing carts.
Ruan: “Shelter and fodder through the spring market. Afterward we negotiate again. This payment doesn't lease the orchard for life.”
Ye: “You can repair carts, but don't count earnings you haven't made yet.”
Rang nods and checks the settled deposit. If two sacks survived, the remaining twelve cover the winter. Otherwise someone must voluntarily contribute money of their own.
You: “How will the carrying ban be enforced?”
Ruan: “I live above the gate and can see the yard. Xu keeps the written terms. No saddle at all, including an empty one used to evade the wording.”
Rang lays the damaged buckle on the table without arguing about an empty saddle. He agrees to replace the latch to the measured size and remains responsible for the beam repair he owes.
Xu lays the retirement papers beside a separate employment contract. Eleven's place is funded by the station's existing budget, without requiring anyone to accompany it as unpaid labor.
Xu: “No freight, riders or forced jumping displays. The receiving carer signs each condition.”
Ye: “Who is the contract for?”
Xu: “There's a six-month care vacancy. You may apply if you wish. Wages are separate from Eleven's fodder allowance.”
Rang: “She's the apprentice I trained.”
Ye: “I remember what you taught me. I still need to choose where I work.”
You ask what happens after six months. Xu confirms that the station's obligation continues whether she renews or leaves. A deer needing years of care cannot bind her indefinitely.
Rang asks about letters. Ye says she will write when she can, but will not accept a new duty to report to him daily. Xu distinguishes that from the actual job.

Xu inspects the verified northern path and watches Eleven walk unladen near the upper orchard gate. It does not limp, but the wound still needs observation. These few steps cannot establish permanent safety.
Xu: “Release means relinquishing ownership. No paper kept in reserve to reclaim it when hauling capacity runs short.”
Rang: “What if it comes back?”
Ye: “Respond to the situation then. Returning wouldn't mean it volunteered to work.”
Ruan: “My upper gate opens for this passage. The fields remain fields. The deer can't grant itself permission to eat the crops.”
Asked whether the wild herd will accept it, Xu shakes his head. Route, mobility and authorized release can be verified. The herd's response cannot.
Rang takes the bell from his bag, holds it through the wrapping for a long while, then hands it to Ye.
Rang: “Don't leave it with me. I know it'll come at the sound. Sometimes my hand moves before I think.”
After the upper gate opens, Eleven waits at the threshold. A deer on the slope looks over and returns to grazing. Rang moves forward before Ye asks him to wait.
Rang: “Before, I'd ring the bell and it would know to move.”
Ye: “There isn't a load waiting for it now. Let it look before moving.”
Eleven sniffs the grass beside the gate, crosses slowly and stops again. Ruan waits until its hind hoof is clear before closing, without asking anyone to drive it toward the herd.
Rang: “I still owe you the beam. I'd like to watch its first day, then come back to repair it.”
Ruan: “All right. Agree on when you'll return. What worries me is another disappearance, not being asked for a day.”

He agrees on the morning he will return. You may stay to observe if your health and existing obligations allow. Leaving means reporting only what you witnessed, without claiming to know tomorrow's result.

Ruan settles freight loss, expenses and the investigation fee item by item. Ye lays the damaged strap beside the record. She corrects her own false statement without borrowing someone else's signature to make the report look complete.
Xu: “Eleven goes into supervised care, with no saddle before review is completed.”
Rang: “That isn't retirement yet.”
Xu: “It isn't. I'll tell you the date and responsible officer once confirmed, rather than invent a timetable.”
Rang: “May I visit?”
Xu: “With the designated carer, following their instructions about the wound.”
Ruan confirms that the commission is paid once and the remaining freight fund returned. Further help would require a new request; the original three stones do not purchase unlimited promises.
The file may include a statement you actually authorize, or stop with the commission report. Nobody signs for an injured person unable to respond, and others' independent statements remain in place.
On Eleven's first morning in the orchard, Rang replaces the shelter latch. The deer reaches for leaves through the fence, watches the hammering briefly, then turns its nose back toward the branch.
Rang: “I thought it would keep looking for the old road.”
Ruan: “Perhaps it will. First repair the fence. You don't need to decide what it ought to be thinking today.”
Ye wants to move the branch. Ruan asks her to get the tree owner's permission first. She laughs, asks, then moves it.
Ruan: “Winter care is funded and freight losses settled. Replacement salt still needs transport. Keeping the deer here doesn't arrange all that by itself.”
Rang: “We'll discuss spring before the final day arrives.”

The agreement covers this winter. Eleven no longer carries freight. Rang still needs work to repair his roof and still owes the beam. Work continues in the yard without someone casually loading the deer again.

On arrival, the receiving carer checks Eleven's wound and familiar feed bowl before reading the carrying ban. Travel will pause for rest as needed. Responsibility begins at handover, not only at the station gate.
Ye packs her own belongings and accompanies them under the six-month contract. Her pay, rest and term are recorded separately. Eleven's continuing care does not depend on endless renewals from her.
Ye declines the post. The station carer signs independently, confirming that her absence does not reduce Eleven's place or care.
Rang: “Don't put this bowl right against a wall. It'll overturn it. Let me show you.”
The carer watches the demonstration and asks how Eleven reacted when the saddle first hurt. Rang admits it kept looking back at his hands, which he dismissed as impatience without checking.
Rang: “I keep wanting to say again that I raised it.”
Ye: “People know. Today you can pass what you've learned to the person taking over.”
He adjusts the bowl and does not follow the lesson with another request to keep the deer.

Ye records that Eleven remains visible among the pines at dusk. It has neither immediately joined the herd nor returned to the gate for the bell. Her account ends where observation ends, without guaranteeing the unseen future.

Xu supplies the release registration so searchers will not capture it as escaped sect property. Ruan records that release does not grant unlimited access to crops; later problems will still need attention.
Rang: “If I call now, it might still come back.”
Ye: “It might. But you've given me the bell.”
Rang looks at her bag and does not reach for it. His agreed beam-repair date remains recorded. Releasing the deer has not released his other obligations.
You observe from the human path until morning without using a lead to decide Eleven's distance. What you see is added to the account; uncertainty remains marked as such.
You report the completed release to the village. Later developments are attributed to Ye's observations rather than written as your own presence.

The retirement review begins with the broken buckle, saddle pad and freight account on the table. No invented bandits enter the file. Eleven is not described as living in an orchard whose agreement was never signed.
Xu: “This is supervised care with a carrying ban during review. The final retirement decision is pending.”
Rang: “I gave it orders for eleven years. Waiting for news feels like doing nothing.”
Ruan: “Then repair the beam. It's broken regardless of when the review ends.”
She puts a hammer on the counter. Rang checks its handle and asks where the timber is, without reaching for the bell.

Ye's correction enters the case independently. Other statements are included only as actually authorized. The commission and freight account are settled; future help must be requested anew. The road remains difficult, but its losses no longer require an imaginary bandit to explain them.
life.full_rewrite.life_story_courier_cac: An overturned cart lies outside the old waystation. As you shelter from the rain, a courier named Xu Yan calls from the doorway. His swollen ankle strains his shoe. He points to the empty compartments and explains that the missing goods are entrusted cargo.
Xu: “Three cases rolled into the drain. I can't get down there on this ankle. If you'll help, let me show you the payment terms first.”

His book lists medicine, a technique rubbing and a cultivation manuscript. The sender has authorized one recovery payment: two pills, study of the rubbing, or study of the manuscript. The written originals must still reach their recipients.
You: “Can the sealed cases be opened for that?”
Xu: “The authorization lets me check, open and reseal them. It doesn't allow unrestricted taking. Whether you can learn the material depends on your abilities.”
He waits for you to read it. The drain is fast and slippery; willingness does not guarantee recovery, and the payment cannot be collected before the work is done.
All three cases are caught behind a broken branch, their seals matching the book. You carry them under the eaves. Xu dries and checks each before opening them under the sender's authorization.
Xu: “Everything is here. Choose one and I'll record it now, without making you wait for my next delivery.”
You: “Can I take the written material?”
Xu: “Study it here, then return the original. I can't teach what I don't understand. Don't force material beyond your cultivation for the sake of a reward.”
The pills are two actual items for you to keep. Study is limited to material you have not learned and can presently use. Xu prepares the resealing materials and waits.
Xu hands over two pills and records payment after you wrap and pack them. The remaining medicine and original texts are resealed for their intended recipients.
Xu: “Thank you for going down there. When the rain eases, I'll ask someone to help right the cart. Taking your payment doesn't make you owe me another job.”
You study the rubbing against your existing training until you can independently reproduce the eligible technique. Xu refills the lamp rather than pretending to confer the skill himself.
The original goes back into its case, and the study authorization is marked fulfilled. You leave with the learned skill, without also collecting pills or manuscript study.

The manuscript's circulation method suits your present qualifications. You study its scope and limits before returning the original. The new method joins what you already know rather than erasing earlier training.
Xu checks the pages and records study as the sole payment before resealing. The manuscript, medicine and rubbing still have their own recipients.

When you leave the waystation, the three cases remain missing. Xu returns the unpaid authorization to his book and prepares to find someone else who can search. No medicine or text changes hands, and you are not asked to acknowledge cargo never recovered.
